Uniform Title: Jñānasiddhyāgama Manuscript: IFP Transcript T0178 Description:
IFP Transcript 178, copied from a manuscript belonging to the Government Oriental Manuscripts Library (GOML), Madras, No. R 16810.
Although this text calls itself an Āgama, it reads more like a treatise dealing with a miscellany of topics related to Śaiva Yoga.
For full bibliographic details, see the Muktabodha Digital Library, IFP/EFEO collection, at www.muktabodha.org.

Publication Year: 2013 Publication Country: United States The Scripture of the Accomplishment of Gnosis (Jñānasiddhyāgama)

Just as knowledge [perceives] the kingdom and so forth, as the object of knowledge perceives the village, the garland, and the garment; and just as the vital breath perceives the various parts of the wind, and the elephant perceives its own limbs—so too does the Self perceive its own distinctions. || 1 ||
In the various arrangements of the bonds of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa), those impelled by ignorance [raise] the banner;
the sound of the ten-fold roar is the musical instrument, arising from the command of the pure Śaiva.
One should perform the ritual procedure of the ten-limbed [mantra] in accordance with these meanings:
ending in Vedānta, Siddhānta, Nādānta, and Vidyābodha. || 3 ||

Through its divisions ending with Samaya, ending with Chāmbhava, ending with Sahamudrikā, ending with Tattva, ending with Sādhaka, and ending with Bodhaka, it culminates in the Supreme (Parāntaka). || 4 ||
It is established that there are sixteen ends, beginning with Śiva and ending with Muktaka;
for each individual end is always seen to arise from accomplishment through its connection [to the preceding].
For the sake of liberation, each successive stage of perception becomes eternal;
in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the supreme state, there is that supreme perception.
When the state of equilibrium has become tranquil, one should behold Śiva, who is higher than the highest;
you [are that] in that state—this is the vision of the Vedānta.
The Conclusion: Now, through the pure yoga of the eight limbs of mantra,
one should perceive Śiva— the end of the knower, the known, and the knowledge— by means of liberation as its limit.
Thus, in the eternal Ananta, they dance the dance of Śambhu;
this is the vision of the perfected goal through the meaning of the divine scripture.
Up to the end of the sound (nādānta).
The stages beginning with *medhā* and ending with *nādānta* are joined by the supreme [levels] ending with *śaktyanta*, and those ending with *samanā*.
In the final stage, the supreme power (*parā śakti*) is to be joined to the others; for the practitioner of *nādānta*, there is eternal perfection.
In that regard, the goal of human life has been elucidated by the texts concerning the emergence of differentiation.
In that void, the state of absolute isolation is the Fourth (turya), which is the vision of the individual soul (jīva);
it is the pure, absolute vision.
In this sense, it is said that within the self-luminous consciousness, there is [nothing else]. || 2 ||
When that exists, remaining continuously in it, that which is eternal is illuminated by it.
|| End of Yoga ||

Having remained constantly and perpetually through the yoga of the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅgayoga) for the sake of universal purpose and meditative absorption, [he attained] that which arises from the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
The Self is established in the specific final tenet;
by the practitioner who burns away the various supreme desires, the pure and great purpose is accomplished for the sake of attainment,
ending in truth.
By means of yoga, having joined the mantras— which are visible through the infinite [realms] and designated by the qualities from the arising of *nāda* up to its end—
with the *ke*, *udaka*, *bandha*, and *tāra* [syllables], that vision is truly real.
Until the end of the observance.

Other eight types of hand-gestures (karabhedas) appear through extreme delusion during times of distress; they consist of mere improper chatter and exist in immeasurable varieties across different eras and different languages.

O Beloved, that supreme mantra which abides within the tradition of the Vedānta Āgamas, which brings about the awakening of the Supreme, and which is equal to the various distinctions of mental states— [that is the means].
Ending with Śāmbhava.
In the fivefold Śāmbhava division, which transcends the Tantras, there are the Śāmbhava mudrās;
through the perception of those mudrās and their corresponding cognitions, there is the illumination of true knowledge known as Śāmbhava.
Ending with the mudrā.
In the Tantra, [the Lord] is the end of mudrās, the end of dance, the end of His own essential nature, and the infinite awakener;
then, being united with blisses, there is liberation, and in that state, the manifestation of the supreme Śambhu’s power and perfection.
To the end of reality.
By means of which [power], having joined the three principles within the form of Kuṇḍalinī,
the characteristic of that which ends with the principle of consciousness is established.
p.
3) Ending with the practitioner (sādhaka).
For there is no fear of death in the pure realm of fire for one who is well-bound;
when the moon and sun are bound, the twelvefold rising occurs for the sake of accomplishment within the essence.
Beloved by the piercer.

The impurity that pierces the self, pierces others, and pierces Śiva; it pierces [all], yet it is itself pierced by its own self-bound state. It is the piercer of equanimity, easily attained peace, and the piercer of the bliss of one's true nature.

The piercing of the limbs, the piercing of the end of the division, the piercing that arises from the circle, the piercing with direct perception, the piercing of the solitary one, the piercing of the supreme quality, and the Śāṅkara piercing.
The supreme state of Śambhu.
The future limit.

I am the supreme state of absolute being, the end of the world-devouring, the peace beyond all, the ultimate limit; I am the person who has vomited out the form of the knot and reached the end of the knot, the state of absolute isolation.
You are the state of emptiness within all states, the singular form, the supreme arising, the all-pervading;
at the end, you are the Supreme Śiva, beyond the highest, the bliss of that which is higher than the high.
While living, he possesses liberation, supreme liberation, and the threefold liberation of Śiva;
by his own nature and in his subtle form, he is one who has attained emancipation.

In its extremely subtle essential nature, it is liberation through the meaning of the *mudrā*. At the end of liberation, within the state of the dance and the end of the dance, it is the differentiator for the sake of liberation. Pervading the state of bliss in the dance, it is the Śāmbhava liberation that culminates in final release.
That which is known as "the end of the sixteen" is the pure determination of Śaivism.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Lord of the universe, Śivānanda Maheśvara!
[Reveal] the established doctrine of pure Śaivism, which illuminates the pure void.
What is called pure yoga? It is that which consists of the true meaning of the pure path, the practice of pure Vedānta, and has the form of pure knowledge.
Maheśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, to that which has been thus declared— the meaning of all the scriptures, difficult to attain,
the essence of the purpose of all the Vedas, and higher than the highest.
That which is the ultimate reality, supreme in form, and likewise born from the Supreme Bindu— that is called the twelfth principle, extending from Parāparā up to Dhātṛ. (31)

Higher than the highest is that which has transcended the other; the power born from that consists of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, and the power born from those is the source of manifestation.
Within knowledge, will, and one's own activity, Śiva and Śakti [reside]; Sadāśiva, Nāda, and Bindu—these six principles, though described in their distinctions, have not been fully revealed.
Likewise, from Maheśa, who is ever auspicious, there was the birth of Rudra; and just as Viṣṇu [arose], so then the Self-born (Brahmā) was produced.
All the principles (tattvas) have been revealed as they are described in the rules for the time of creation:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
Bindu and Nāda are twofold Śiva, who is higher than the highest; in their midst is the source of all, situated within the quartet beginning with Druhiṇa (Brahmā).
Sādākhya is called Bindu, and Nāda is said to be Sakala-akala;
Śiva, Śakti, and Para are the three, and the fourth is Parātpara.
It is proclaimed as consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*);
indeed, this purification of the essence of reality (*tattvasāra*) is divided into two parts, the higher and the lower. (38)
The Sakala, the Niṣkala, and the Ubhaya—these are the three groups.
The three belonging to the Trivarga are situated in the middle; they are Ātma-vidyā and the triad of Śiva.
That which is declared as the twenty-sixfold division is the means for the arising of those three.
In the principles (tattva) of will, knowledge, and action, there are nine powers arising from them;
likewise, [the powers] beginning with Śakti and ending with Parā arise from the summit of the Prāsāda.
The ninefold power is declared by the injunctions; it is the Navamūlāgama-yāmala, as well as that very Śāmbhava-tattvasiddha-śāstra.
The fifth is declared to be Śāmbhava; that is the purification for the purpose of initiation. (42)
The Śāmbhava [initiation] is characterized by truth; the pure Śāmbhava is superior;
and the unmentioned [forms] are also Śāmbhava—such is the definition of the Śāmbhava [initiations].
The meaning of Vedānta is new knowledge, the supreme and auspicious Siddhānta;
it is called Dakṣiṇācāra, which prescribes the conduct ordained by the Veda. || 44 ||
The contrary left-hand path (*vāmamārga*) belongs to the Śākta tradition, while this [right-hand path] falls within the domain of Śaivism.
In the midst [of these] are the powers of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), along with the goddess Mantrikā.
The mantras arise from Śakti; the remainder is the speech of Śakti, and the fifth is likewise.
Parā has the form of that which is beyond the supreme (parāt para); Śiva-Śakti arises from that.
The syllable Oṃ, which arises from Nāda and Bindu, is the form of the pure reality;
it is pure knowledge, or rather, the pure cause of Śakti.
The seed of knowledge is the supreme form, the syllable Oṃ, the Lord who is the Sovereign;
it is the form of Śiva known as the Eternal (Sat), arising from the fifth kalā.
The letters A, U, and M, along with Bindu and Nāda, are present within the five;
the syllable Oṃ, which possesses all forms, arises from the fifth.
The extremely subtle sound (nāda) has arisen, and from that subtle [sound] the drop (bindu) is produced;
they behold that as the essence of the letter *M*, while the letter *U* is the arising of the middle.
The letter *A* is the primordial speech (*ādivāk*) produced as Vaikharī, the fivefold means;
in its center is Īśāna, the Lord, who is Rudra, whose essence is Viṣṇu, and who is most abundant.
The fifth is Sakalīśakti; likewise, there is that which arises from the five Śantis.
For the purpose of the fivefold acts beginning with creation, there is the manifestation of the deities of Brahmā and the others.
The Vaiṣṇava [tantra] is one ten-millionth part of the Brahman [tantra], and the Rudra-bheda is equal to that;
there are many divisions, numbering twenty-eight.
The fifth is declared to be Sādākhya; Nāda and Bindu are the fourth.
[Then there are] the powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action, and Māyā—thus it is fivefold. (54)
Sadāśiva, Nādaśiva, Parāśiva at the end of Nāda, Śiva in the form of mantra, and the Self as the fifth Śiva—that is Śiva. (55)
Formless and beyond you is the letter Śa, which possesses three supreme portions;
it is at the end of Parā, at the end of Paranāda, at the end of Śiva, and beyond the three supreme ones.
At the time of creation, for the sake of the three dots (bindus), there arises the form of a triangle;
that place is the principle of the Bindu (baindava-tattva), originating from the three seed-syllables (bījas).
The form of Nāda and Bindu arises from the power of Bindu;
it consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning with the end of Nāda and ending with the earth element.
In the center of that, there is the form of the Praṇava, likewise arisen from the soul of its seed-syllable;
it rests within the great center of the triangle, supported by four syllables.
Thus, the seed-syllable situated in the center, the supreme portion, the seed of desire, is known as the seed of liberation; it is the supreme essence of all mantras.
The seed-syllable of the triangle exists in a threefold form as the source of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
it is produced from the Praṇava in the center, and in the Atharva Veda, it is the "tooth-tooth" syllable.
All that is pervaded by Kuṇḍalinī, the cause of the meaning of all principles;
she is the three Vedas of the ritual sections (karmakāṇḍa) and the Atharva Veda in the form of knowledge.
The supreme beyond the supreme, the non-duality of the two selves who are completely tranquil,
which is equal to that [Brahman], is the destroyer of the ten states for the sake of the vow and for the attainment of perfection.
For the sake of accomplishing each respective true path, there is the practice of that respective true path;
such is the Great Vidyā, which abides in the injunctions of the Vedānta.
The Vedānta and the Śaiva Siddhānta are one in their unity beyond Śiva;
this is the pure Śaivism that is self-realized and embodies the path of pure existence.
If that white Veda consists of four Vedas and five divisions,
and the collection of letters beginning with 'a' resides therein, then that speech is born from Bhava. (66)
From Brahmā up to Īśāna, there are the five causes consisting of the *kalās*;
from Sadyojāta onwards, the Creator [Brahmā] extends up to Īśāna as Sadāśiva.
The form arises from the twenty-eighth [letter] situated in the middle of the fifth;
it is the power of the supreme Śakti consisting of Bindu and Nāda, and thus the Śiva-Śakti is fivefold.
In the midst of those, one who is capable may [expound] that which arises from the twenty-eight Āgamas of the Mūlatantras,
as well as that which arises from the nine Tantrāgamas belonging to each respective internal [tradition].

The fifth is the function of eloquence (vāgmīvṛtti), which is power; likewise, in the center is that which arises from the Vedas, containing all phonemes and the meaning of its own scriptures, as well as the point (bindu) arising from the principle (tattva).
The commentary on the *Divyāgama*: *Tantrāvatāraviveka*.
Regarding the secret meaning of the nine Āgamas, there is the arising of the twenty-eight [deities]. (71)
The state beyond the beyond (parātpara) is twofold, endowed with Śiva and Śakti;
it takes the form of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, and is joined with the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti).
The divisions of Śiva and Sādākhya arise from the manifestation of the Sādākhya form. || 72 ||
Thus, this sequence of meanings constitutes its manifestation;
it is the ninefold scripture, the purpose of which is power, arising from the *Yāmala* in nine divisions and manifold ways. (73)
Śiva, Śakti, Bindu, Nāda, and Sādākhya as the fifth—these twenty-eight [principles] at the root are the cause everywhere in the scripture. (74)
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna as the fifth—these are the respective tantras taught, namely the twenty-eight scriptures beginning with the Kāmika. (75)
Scripture is the arrival of success; the threefold scripture is the arrival of the essence.
It is divided by the *Kālottara* and other texts, which serve as secondary branches of its root.
For the sake of its various divisions, there are more than two hundred [tantras] beginning with the Kāmika;
[it contains] the scripture of the Vedasāra-āgama and the Vedānta which is the conclusion of the āgamas.

The embodied and the single-formed are declared to be distinguished by the Vedas and the Āgamas; the scripture that stands in the midst of the fourfold classes of speech shall be proclaimed as arising from all [of them]. (78)
The Mūlāgama, the Sanmārga, the Sahamārga, the Śivagama, the Śivasṛṣṭi consisting of five forms, and the Śaktyāgama as the eighth. || 79 ||
Sādākhya is proclaimed by Pārvatī; in the Tantras there are nine Tāras; Devasāra consists of ten parts, and Gaṇeśasāra consists of eleven.
Vāma, Gaurava, and their divisions, Gautama, Gaṇeśvara, Nandikeśa as the fifteenth, and Aindusāra as the excellent sixteenth. || 81 ||
Then follows the Gaurīsārāgama, after that the Pañcāmaheśāsāra,
then the Aghorasārāgama, and after that the Viṣṇusāra.
Then after that, the Brahmasāra; then the Samayasāraka;
and likewise the Mahodbhavodbhava, which originates from the incarnation of Rudra. || 83 ||
Beauty, the essence of the perfected ones, and the great mountain as the sixth; this is the view equal to space.
Sādākhya was proclaimed by Pārvatī as the ninth incarnation of Ātmantra. || 84 ||
The essence of the gods (devasāra) is one-tenth of that, and from that, the gaurava is considered equal;
thus, there are twenty-eight varieties which are the cause of the primary materials (mūlapādāna). || 85 ||
It is known as the twenty-fourth, and the twenty-eighth is the differentiator;
the other eight divisions are the conceptualization declared by the eight Vidyeśvaras.
Thus, there are twenty-eight divisions; this is the essence of the introduction to the Tantra, the true path and the path of endurance, as proclaimed in the original divine scriptures.
This treatise is the word of Śiva, which brings down the root-tantra;
it is proclaimed as the great [teaching] for Nandikeśa, bringing down a portion of the tantra. (88)
The essence of the meaning of the thousand divine scriptures, the most excellent among essences,
the auspicious root scripture, the true path, the path of all paths— the Śiva-āgama. (89)
The intention is that the power of Śiva’s creative emanation resides in the Sādākhya [tattva]; this is the view of Pārvatī.
O pure Śaivas, there is unity between the two descents of the Tantra; salutations! 90.
I consider the Śuddha-Śaiva Āgama to be supreme, as well as other Tantras, such as the Nandikeśa, which is the highest secret that sets forth the knowledge of Yoga. || 91 ||
The Śiva-Sāṃkhya, the Yoga-Sāṃkhya, and the Sāṃkhya—these are the two systems of the dualistic Āgamas;
the Nirvāṇa-Sāra is the first essence of Sāṃkhya knowledge, and the [other] is the second.
O Goddess, Guha [taught] the essence of reality (tattvasāra), which has a threefold division, as well as the cause, the pure path, and that which is superior to the throat. 93.
In the Śaiva Bhedāgama, that which is the direct entrance to liberation is declared to be the Pūrvakāṇḍa, the subtle Śāmbhava Siddhānta. 94.
The Uttara-kāṇḍa follows after; then there is the Kāmika and so forth:
the Kāmika, the Yogaja, the Cintya, and likewise the Kāraṇatvajita.
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabhedaka, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svāyaṃbhuva, and Anala. (96)
Vīra, Raurava, Mākuṭa, and likewise Vimala;
Candrajñāna, Bimba, Prodgīta, and likewise Lalita. || 97 ||
The Siddha, the Sāntāna, the Sārva, the Pāramaiśvarya,
the Kiraṇa, and the Vātula— these are the twenty-eight Saṃhitās.
Likewise, there are five [tantras] beginning with Kāmika, which arise from the mouth of Sadyojāta;
the fifth division, beginning with Dīpta, arises from the mouth of Vāmadeva.
The fifth division, beginning with Vijaya, originated from the mouth of Aghora;
likewise, the five beginning with Raurava were proclaimed from the mouth of Tatpuruṣa.
The eighth division, beginning with *prodgīta*, was proclaimed by the mouth of Īśāna;
thus, there are twenty divisions of forms in the sequence of the scriptures and the *Āgamas*. (101)
Two hundred and twenty-four are the measured divisions of those respective [schools];
the twenty-eight other divisions constitute the conceptualization of the Śaiva Siddhānta. (102)
The previously mentioned twenty-eight [tantras] are to be understood as having four quarters;
otherwise, the Āgama is said to be twofold, namely the Śivadharmottara.
The various scriptures are for the purpose of engaging in diverse practices and distinguishing between various philosophical systems;
the Pauṣkara, Yoga, Sāṃkhya, Tattvasāra, and others are distinguished by their specific meanings.
The Ākekārthāgama, the Saṃkhyā, the Catuṣpādā, and others;
O Goddess, the Kālottara, the Skandakālottara, and the Dvayottara. (105)
The *Sarvajñānottara*, the *Saṃkhyā*, and so forth—these are the enumerations of knowledge;
they were proclaimed in various Śaiva Āgamas for the sake of engaging with the diverse Śaiva traditions. (106)
The enumeration of the two infinite scriptures, the conceptualization of the beginning, time, and the Lord;
and through the application of mantra, tantra, ritual action, and yoga, there arises the knowledge that determines the meaning of Śiva. || 107 ||
The Śaiva reality arises from the Śākta, and likewise the Śākta arises from the Śaiva;
having encapsulated both, one performs the piercing of the supreme Prāsāda-mantra. 108.
The unity of the two supreme palaces is proclaimed by Śambhu;
it is the foot consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which manifests as white and red. (109)
Then there is unity, the reality of rest, that state of being, the supreme station, the Śiva-principle consisting of Śakti, and the Supreme Śiva who transcends all principles. || 110 ||
The Kulārṇava, the Kulottīrṇa, the Kulasadbhāva, the Kulāmṛta,
the meaning of the supreme and highest scriptures, and the teaching of the Kālīkākulam.
"By the tradition of the perfected nectar, success [is attained]," and so forth—this is the Śākta and Vāma [tradition].
The distinction between the two Navayāmalas is manifold, according to their respective divisions. (112)
The Śākta, the Śāmbhava, and [the other] are the causes of their connection; this scripture, known as the "Triple Confluence," is said to extend to the end of the Traividya. 113.
That which is known as Pure Śaiva arises from the Pure Śāmbhava;
the unification of Prāsāda and Parā constitutes the two-fold Pure Śaiva. (114)
The Śākteya, the Śāmbhava, the Śaiva, the Vedānta, and other Āgamas; likewise, the Nādānta, the Nāṭānta, the Sakya, and the Drānta-Śāmbhava. (115)
Thus, the purification of the nine ends is the pure Śaiva illumination;
it begins with Sadyojāta, culminates in the Praṇava, and concludes with the Mudrās as its means of accomplishment.
The division of the sixteenfold [system] has been proclaimed;
each one of the Kālāmukha observances is said to consist of five parts. 117.
There are eight divisions of Bhairava and sixty-four subdivisions;
Vāma has sixteen [divisions], and its subdivisions are manifold.
The twelfth is the Śaiva division, and its specific sub-division is the Śivādvaita;
the divisions of Lakulīśvara are proclaimed to be fivefold. (119)
There are sixty Śaiva scriptures that distinguish [the traditions] and whose purpose is the meaning of the sacred texts. || 120 ||

The various millions of parts, which consist of the meanings of the scriptures regarding the different forms [of the deity], become the power of the Bindu; thus is the Vāgbhava [syllable] conceived in the scripture. (121)
The Bindu is the source of discord; the scriptures are the instigators of the knowledge of others.
That scripture is the supreme secret, higher than the highest. (122)
The meaning of the various different scriptures is conceived as having four parts;
between the infinite scriptures, the essence consists of twenty-eight [verses].
(12) Rooted in that is the scripture (*āgama*), its divisions are ninefold; this is the fundamental conceptualization (*kalpanā*).
It is the scripture that introduces the *tantra* for the sake of the essential meaning of the respective essences. 124.

For the sake of the secret meaning of the Vedas and Āgamas, which causes wonder at the conclusion of the Vedas and Āgamas; for the sake of illuminating the pure Śaiva [truth], it is born from the pure Śāmbhava.
Thus, the Śuddhaśaiva has been revealed as the essence; the essence of essences has been revealed.
The secret more secret than the secret, the essence of the very essence, has been revealed. (126)
The Śāmbhava is [attained] through the Śākta, and the Śaiva is [attained] through the Śāmbhava; O Śiva, the Śāktaka is attained through the Śāmbhava.
This unity of the two is accessible through the realization of the Vedānta tenets, and it is accessible through the knowledge of that very Vedānta tenet.

[He is] non-different from those who differ regarding the Vedānta tenets, [yet he is] liberation consisting in rest within the Vedānta tenets; this is the pure Śaiva system, the founder of this scripture, the supreme Śiva, Vyomakeśa, whose nature is the light of pure emptiness. (127)
The true meaning of the pure path has been illuminated by pure knowledge;
the true meaning of the pure Vedānta is this auspicious reality. 128.
The supreme Guru, whose form consists of pure gnosis, who transcends both the higher and the lower,
who is beyond the portions of pure yoga, and who is the supreme Śiva culminating in the state of Unmanā.

O Goddess of beautiful countenance, O Śaṅkarī, this which has been declared as the previously mentioned latent impression (vāsanā) is for the sake of engaging in pure Śaiva practice; therefore, remain composed. 130.
In the *Jñānasiddhyāgama*, the first chapter, the section on the introduction to the tantra (*tantrāvatārasaṃhitā*), is completed.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, Mahādeva, Great Yogi, Maheśvara!
O Maheśāna, Great Counselor, you are praised; I am Śivā. (1)
Having established the supreme convention of inconceivable gnosis as the ultimate,
Sadāśiva created the Prāsāda [mantra], which has the meaning of the convention of non-existence. (2)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this inconceivable matter—the oneness of Śiva and the Self, born of Śiva;
the knowledge of the Lord, the fetter, and the bound soul, which is both partless and yet differentiated by conceptual thought.
The Discrimination of the Characteristics of Śiva:
O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe the characteristics of Śiva in brief.
Śiva is higher than the highest, subtle, free from conceptual construction, and stainless. (4)
Beyond the Tattvas is the Supreme Danta; beyond the Turya is the Supreme Śiva;
beyond Nāda is the end of Nāda, the eternal bliss, Sadāśiva. || 5 ||
It is non-enjoyable, stainless knowledge, indestructible, and devoid of selfhood.
Purity, pure convention, the pure self manifested by its own radiance,
the sixfold division of the paths, convention, pervasion, and the determination of pervasion.
The Prāsāda, the supreme mantra, and the Parā-mantra are unified as one;
the union of Prāsāda and Parā is red, white, and blended.
The characteristic of the feet is twofold: red, white, and mixed.
Your foot is thus red, while my foot is indeed white.
The cause for the sake of enjoyment and liberation is the [union of] the red and the white;
distinguished by the radiance of the red and the white, it is the supreme reality signifying Śiva and Śakti.
The phoneme consisting of the two letters *sa* and *śa*, arising from the *bindu* and *nāda*, is known as the *ātman-mantra*, the supreme syllable of the Prāsāda. (11)
The *Śivalakṣaṇaviveka* is completed.
The Palace of Seclusion.
The syllable *prā* is the knowledge of Śiva; the syllable *sā* is said to be the goal (liberation).
Together with the syllable *dam*, this three-syllabled [mantra] is thus described as the very nature [of the Self]. || 12 ||

The path (adhvan) is the conventional way (*saṃketamārga*), which consists of its own essential nature (*svarūpaka*): it is the phoneme (*varṇa*), the energy-portion (*kalā*), the word (*pada*), the principle (*tattva*), the mantra, and indeed the world-sphere (*bhuvana*). || 13 ||
All association with the arts and so forth, as well as the forms of their cessation and so on;
these are Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the fifth is Atīta.

Having attained the self that is beyond the inner self and the supreme—the self of knowledge, not limited by its own form—and having assumed the body of all mantras, perform the fivefold activity as Śiva. 15.
The powers of will, knowledge, and action, which perform the fivefold cosmic acts through the power of will,
constitute the triad of causes— will, knowledge, and action— which is the Lord.
The fifth is Nāda; for the sake of Śakti, there are the three causes beginning with Ādi.
The seat is the power of the bindu, and its own linga is the power of the nāda;
one should contemplate the Self as the union of bindu and nāda, the bindu-repha, which is higher than the highest.
The supreme [vibration] resides in the center of the *bindu*; it consists of *vaikharī* and the others, as well as the cloud-like [sound].
*Vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, *paśyantī*, and that which is designated as *sūkṣmā* [are the four stages]. (19)
Vaikharī is the object of the sense of hearing; Madhyamā, however, is conceptual; the third, Paśyantī, is non-conceptual; and the final one, Para, is the cause.
The scripture for the accomplishment of knowledge:
those who possess the power of action perceive the subtle arising that originates from the center.
In the syllable *ukāra*, that which is produced in the middle [state] arises; in the syllable *akāra*, it is manifested as *vaikharī*.
Joined with the syllable *graḥ*, it consists of the letters *haṃ*, *oṃ*, and *aṃ*;
it resembles the essence of the *bindu* and has the form of the *baindava-tattva*.
One perceives the subtle arising within the Bindu at the letter A;
thus, the convention of the activity of speech, beginning with Vaikharī, emerges from the phonemes.
The letter U, the letter U, the letter M, the Bindu, and the Nāda as the fifth;
[these correspond to] the mind, the intellect, the ego, the consciousness, and so forth. 24.
Everything arises within the Bindu at that time, and likewise, it is of the nature of the Bindu;
at the time of dissolution, she who is crooked like a riverbank arises from the Praṇava in its midst.
Oṃ, Āḥ, and Māyā are the three bonds; likewise, Kuṇḍalī consists of these three.
Therein, in the center, is Kuṇḍalinī, arising from Iḍā and Piṅgalā.
Between the iḍā and piṅgalā is the one whose nature is called suṣumnā;
within the suṣumnā is the subtle entry into the wonderful nāḍī.
Situated within the center of one's own body amidst the variegated channels, and endowed with both prāṇa and apāna, that which is beyond the duality of prāṇa and apāna is the supreme cause. (28)
The letter *ha* is the nature of Śiva, and the letter *sa* is said to be Śakti;
between the letters *ha* and *sa* is the supreme refuge in the form of the *bindu*.
Nāda is situated within the bindu; Śiva is situated within nāda;
within Śiva is the tranquil, beyond tranquility, the supreme beyond the supreme.
The entirely arisen twofold power consists of Māyā and Kuṇḍalinī;
through the divisions of Māyā and Kuṇḍalinī, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings [is manifested]. 31.
(16) From the knot arise the [tattvas] beginning with Kalā, Kāla, Vidyā, Rāga, and Indriya; as well as Guṇa, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, Citta, the Akṣas, Mātrās, and the Bhūtas. || 32 ||
The Kuṇḍalinī energy is Māyā, which follows the course of karma; the effects of this [energy] consist of Nāda, Bindu, and so forth—such is the constitution of the world. (33)
The distinction between the sixteen digits (kalās), arising from the root Kuṇḍalinī,
has the form of the sixteen digits and is established within the moonstone.
Therein, the power of the two sixteenth [vowels] is established in the body of the Moon;
the other mantra, consisting of the form of the digits (kalā), is the supreme syllable of the Prāsāda.
The letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the bindu;
the half-moon, the nirodhī, and the nāda;
the śakti, the vyāpinī, the samanā, and likewise the unmanā.
The net of bonds extends as far as the limit of Samanā; beyond that is the Supreme Śiva at the end of Unmanā. || 37 ||
The fifth row [of deities] in the temple contemplates the foundation, the expansion, the completion arising from the ritual action, and stability.
The letter *a* has the nature of the vowel; the letter *u* is the form of the Lord (Īśa);
the letter *m* has the nature of poison; and the Bindu alone is the supreme syllable *pha*.
The form of the half-moon is likewise for cessation; that [form] is a triangle, with two dots (*bindu*) and the resonance (*nāda*), and its counterpart is the *pratīhala*.
Halā, Mitrāṅgita, Śakti, Vyāpinī, and there Śūlakam;
Kubjikā, Vyomarūpī, Anantā, and so forth—these are the six powers.
The six dots form the shape of a crest; its tip is [marked] with a probe.
That is the partless reality (niṣkala-tattva) of Śiva, established for the purpose of the ritual placement (prasthāra). || 42 ||
In the center, there is the extensive sequence of pervasion consisting of six parts;
it is the state of each of the two to be joined, the liberation, and the firm sequence. (43)
O dear one, having seen the stability of the two others at the limit beyond, that which consists of cultivation is then the palace of the conventional continuity of contemplation. 44.
The path is sixfold; therein, the word, the phoneme, and the weapon arise from emission.
Because everything has the nature of power (śakti), these are the forms of the signifier. || 45 ||
This triad of dyads in the form of the expressible consists of Śakti and Śiva. || 46 ||

That wheel, which is the primary cause consisting of the nature of clay, is the auxiliary cause; it is the source of the relationship between the signified and the signifier, and it arises from the impurity of *bindu*. || 47 ||
The origin of the earthen vessel was described by the Kulālas as being from clay alone;
thereafter, the knot in the form of clay is situated within the wheel of Kuṇḍalinī. 48.
He brings about that world of moving and non-moving beings in every direction;
the causal power of the Pervasive One consists of will, knowledge, and action. (49)
The fifth function is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which is accomplished by Brahmā and the others;
the Bindu consists of the entire creation, and within it arises the phoneme (*varṇa*).
The inconceivable Kuṇḍalinī energy, arisen within all,
exists for the sake of action.
Creation is for the sake of binding the self to reality; maintenance is the means for its experience. || 51 ||
The separation of the self from that [reality], its dissolution, the performance of action at that time, the stable state, and concealment are thus described. 52.
He performs the fourth activity, which is the means for bestowing grace.
(p. 18) Thus, for the sake of the fifth activity, the five divine [deities] and so forth are established. 53.
These five, however, constitute the subtle function of the solitary *aga*:
awakening, purifying, deluding, binding, and likewise praising. (54)
At the time of the great dissolution, however, the crooked portion arises from that [source],
consisting of the collection of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, which constitutes the embodied form.
The form of knowledge has the nature of Śiva, while the forms are the powers (śaktis);
that reality which is the union of knowledge and action is the essential nature known as Sādākhya.
Maheśa is the embodiment of that reality in which knowledge is subordinate and action is predominant;
Śaṅkara is the goal of pure knowledge, in whom action is truly perfected through yoga. 57.
When desire predominates, Viṣṇu is said to be the principle (tattva) of Brahmā;
therefore, the distinctions such as desire and so forth constitute the very nature of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Rudra and Viṣṇu [preside over] that which is declared in the ordinances regarding the authority for enjoyment during the kalpa;
likewise, in the center is the power of the Bindu, arising from the power of Māyā.

In the midst of the power of Māyā is the power [of Śakti], and from that [power] arises [the universe]. When the power of desire (kāmya-śakti) resides in its own center, this is Māyā, and from it arises [the world].

Likewise, the fourfold impurity (caturmala) is to be pierced, and that which exceeds it is concealment (tirodhāna). Thus, the fivefold impurity is the bondage of the fetters (pāśabandha) of Śakti; so it is called.
Thus, having performed the ritual of dismemberment and having thus respectfully reached a definitive conclusion, [he addressed] the God of gods, Maheśāna, Mahāyogin, Maheśvara. (62)
That mantra which is to be grasped as the essence is said to be the form of that mantra.
Śaṅkara said:
Through the nasal sound (nāda) beginning with the sixteenth vowel (bindu), there arises the bindu within one's own nāda.
That form has the shape of the *praṇava* and is established as the five syllables;
it is the single-syllabled Brahman, "Om," the supreme self, the embodiment of one's own nature. (64)
The syllable Oṃ is the nature of Śiva; its fivefold division is pervaded by the root Kuṇḍalinī, which is the self, the mantra, and one's own phonemes.
The Haṃsa-vidyā, the Great Vidyā, together with the Prāsāda-mantra and the Supreme (Parā),
[constitutes] the Prāsāda-para, which is the very embodiment of Śakti.
The oneness of the two, the palace and the beyond, is the Śāmbhava state, born from Śiva;
if [the Bindu] is pierced by the Nāda, it becomes resonant and is found within the Kha.
The form of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, which is the very embodiment of Śiva and Śakti, is the support, the mental object of meditation, and the supreme Śiva. (68)
One should practice with the *bindu* as the foundational seat (*pīṭha*) and the *nāda* as the *liṅga*;
the *bindu* is the differentiated eternal form, while the portion of the *bhaga* is the embodiment of *śakti*.
In the center of the triangle is the syllable *hau*, [representing] Dharma, Haṃsa, Hari, and Śiva;
the Haṃsa is situated in the Bindu within the Nāda on the path of the Haṃsa.
They say that *nāda* is the *liṅga*, and it is declared to be the seat (*pīṭha*) of the *bindu*.
*Nāda* has entered into the center of the *bindu*, and Śiva has entered into the center of *nāda*. (71)
Śakti is situated within Śiva, and Śiva himself is within Śakti;
there is also the distinction of the Parahaṃsa, namely the letters Ha and Hau.
The Haṃsa and the Paramahaṃsa are the two-fold divisions of the Haṃsa;
[the former thinks] "I am indeed the earth, I am the waters, and I am the Lord. (73)
I am the earth, I am fire, I am Hari;
I am the ether, the true reality, I am the Self, and I am the Supreme.
The letter *ha* is the nature of Brahmā; the letter *u* is the form of Viṣṇu;
the letter *ma* is the nature of Rudra; and the *bindu* is indeed Īśvara. (75)
Nāda is declared to be Sadāśiva, and that which transcends Nāda is Paraśiva; it is the supreme reality, the highest object of knowledge, and the very nature of supreme liberation.
The letter *ha* is endowed with the partless (*niṣkala*), while the letter *sa* is the manifest (*sakala*). The letter *ha* is the nature of Śiva, and the letter *sa* is said to be Śakti.
The letter *ha* signifies the sun, the letter *sa* likewise signifies the moon, and the letter *i* signifies fire; thus the triad of lights is proclaimed. (78)
The letter *ha* is said to have the form of a *bindu* between the letters *ka* and *ra*;
within that *bindu* resides the *nāda*, and within the *nāda* resides Śiva. (79)
By means of the *bindu* one proceeds through the *nāda*, and from the resonant state one is split by the void (*kha*).
That reality (*tattva*) resides in the center of Śiva; it is the highest of the high within the midst of all realities.
The Supreme, higher than the highest, subtle, the recipient of supreme liberation, having the form of space, the great void, beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), the Supreme Śiva. || 81 ||
The state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is the moving abode, revealed as the supreme ether;
it is the form of the absolute (parākāra), the syllable Om, whose nature is light.
He is both child and old man, possessing a form with beginning and end, yet devoid of them; he is the seed of knowledge, yoga, and action, and the supreme color beyond all ritual acts.
The syllable Oṃ is the Supreme Self, manifested as the Supreme Power;
therefore, it is Brahman consisting of knowledge, the light whose form is "Oṃ. (84)
The syllable Oṃ consists of the acute, grave, and circumflex accents; it is a curved sound.
Within that sound is the light, and within the light is the mind.
The intellect is contained within the mind; my consciousness is contained within the intellect;
the mind is contained within me; and the mind is contained within the Self.
Time is contained within the Self; within time is the digit (kalā);
within the digit are Nāda and the end of Nāda (*nādānta*); [and] beyond that is Parā. (87)
Knowledge is contained within the Supreme, and Śiva is contained within knowledge;
because it is contained within all, that is Brahman, and that Brahman is higher than the highest.

Thus, for one who has entered within the meaning, there are two *oṃ*s; the syllable *oṃ*, which arises from the Guru and is declared to be the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*) according to the method of the eight limbs of yoga, is the third. (89)
The seven vyāhṛtis, the Gāyatrī, the Sāvitrī, the Prakṛti, the Kṛti,
the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), the four Vedas, the Smṛti, renunciation, and then Maya.
Self-discrimination (*ātma-viveka*) does not arise from various [conditions]; that which has been attained is composed of the nature of illusion (*māyā*).
One should perform the fifth [rite], the binding of the noose whose nature consists of the end of illusion (māyā).
The purification of the noose is the individual soul (jīvātman), while the supreme [purification] is the purification of that state of being a bound soul (paśu). 91.
The supreme [mantra] is to be purified by the praṇava, ending with the syllable Oṃ; it is higher than the guru.
There is nothing higher than the guru, for there is indeed no Śiva other than the guru.
The *Praṇavaviveka* is completed.
Now begins the investigation into the origin of the *liṅga*.
The Praṇava is said to consist of the Bindu and Nāda; it is the source of the Kuṭilākāra (the Crooked Form).
The Kurus [worship] Śiva, who has arisen for the sake of his own power, Kuṭilā. 93.
One should practice that liṅga as the Praṇava, which has the form of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā; it extends from the end of Nāda through the noose of Kalā up to Unmanī, and is superior to that.

The pure path (śuddhādhvan) begins at the end of Samanā, extending to the supreme Śiva at the end of Unmanī; it culminates at the end of that which is proclaimed as the [supreme] state beyond mind (unmanī). 95.
Time, the world, and the phonemes, the path of mantra and the path of words,
and the path of principles— these should be known as the six paths, which constitute the form of Sādākhya. (96)

The path of the arts (kalādhvan) is said to be the wind element; the world-sphere (bhuvana) is the hair of the body; the skin and the letters (varṇa) are the blood; and the path of the feet consists of the channels (nāḍī) and the veins (śirā).
Sadāśiva, whose form consists of the elements as described in the section on the twenty-six principles, is that [reality];
the power that impels its differentiation is called Parā-śakti. (98)
This is Śiva, established in his own essential nature, known as Sādākhya and Udbhava;
he is Sadāśiva, the source of the universe, who abides in the authority over the fivefold cosmic acts.
The supreme seed-syllable is situated in the center; the lines of the triangle represent the breasts and so forth.
One should perform the worship of the female organ (bhaga) and the male organ (liṅga) within the central triangular form.
The *liṅga* is situated in the middle of the *bhaga*, and the *bhaga* is situated in the middle of the *liṅga*.
The *liṅga* is the seat of Sadāśiva, while the pedestal (*pīṭhikā*) is the seat of the *liṅga*.
The pedestal-seat is between the eyebrows; the teacher’s seat is the seat of meditation.
Having meditated thus with the mind, one should then install the Supreme Power (Parāśakti). 102.
The [tantra] called Sādākhya has five divisions; its division arising from sixteen is the twenty-eighth, declared by Maheśa as Naṭarāja, which is the primary one. (103)
Through the will [of Śiva], that which is called the descent of grace (śivasāda) arises; its beginning is born from the fifth.
Maheśa, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and so forth, as well as the five elements, constitute the fifth.
Everything that has arisen is called Sādākhya; one should practice the three causes:
the embodied, the formless, and the embodiment of action, with Śiva as the fifth.
Gaṇeśa is born from Rudra; likewise, his own division is the sixteenth.
Viśākha is also born from Rudra; his own collection consists of one division with six parts.
(23) Gods, asuras, humans, śaktis, ṛṣis, kinnaras, and so forth—
all these have arisen innumerable times from the midst of a single hair-pore of Rudra. 107.
The ten [deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śivatattva arise from the Sādākhya [tattva];
Vedhas is in the western part, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa is in the north.
One should see Aghora in the southern part, Puruṣa as declared in the east, Īśāna in the position of Īśāna, and [Sadyojāta] as declared in the center. (109)
The middle and the tip, as well as the *bindu* and the *nāda*, the tips of the lines are Śiva;
the center of Śiva is for the sake of Śakti—this is the source known as Sādākhya.

Peaceful, seated upon the lotus posture, wearing a crown of the moon, with five faces and three eyes, he bears in his left and right hands a trident, a vajra, a sword, and an axe, while granting protection from fear. 111.
In the left [hand], he holds a nose-rope, a noose, a bell together with a mace, and a goad;
adorned with various ornaments, resembling a crystal gem, it is the gentle reality known as Sāda.

The head of the Goddess is to the south and her beautiful feet to the north; the Gomukha is at the end of the feet where water is applied. With arms joined, the Linga is established in the center situated within the Yoni, resting in the nectar (madhu).
This is the nature of Sadāśiva in the Unmanī state. He who possesses the power of mind (manaśśaktika) should be known as the supreme Śiva, the Unmanī. || 13 ||
Because of its connection with both *mana* and *unmana*, it is designated as *manonmanī*.
In the midst of the eight powers beginning with Vāmā is Manonmanī;
situated in the middle of Manonmanī is the Sādākhya, which is the central Liṅga.
The Liṅga is established as Śiva-Śakti, and likewise as the source of the origin of the world;
it possesses the nine limbs of knowledge and the lotus-limbs, yet it is not possessed of the three wheels.
From that Maheśvara, the world arises as both the phallic portion (liṅgāṃśa) and the vulva portion (bhagāṃśa).
Therein is the four-petaled mūlādhāra, in the center of which are the syllables va, śa, ṣa, sa, and ja.
In the midst of that, she who has the form of a curve, arising from the shape of a triangle,
whose body is enveloped by the roots of the channels, is Kuṇḍalinī, with the sound of a swan. (118)
The vital breath (prāṇa), born from the *praṇava*, is situated in the center in the form of a coil;
it stands within the three *praṇavas*, is of the nature of space, and possesses supreme power.
Valor arises from another; the Supreme is the cause everywhere.
It is a mass of consciousness pervaded by clouds, eternal, and ever-shining with radiance. 120.
Śambhu is the all-pervading cause of the self of all, witnessed by his own entire being;
he is Śambhu’s supreme Śiva, the subtle, all-encompassing Lord.
It is of every color, likewise the mantra, and the embodiment of the mantra in manifold ways;
it is the great mantra of all ten million, the cause consisting of seven million parts.
The eightfold Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) of consciousness, whose primary form is the mantra-body, consists of seventy million great mantras that cause the agitation of the mind. || 123 ||
With one [syllable], he should contemplate the innate mantra, the supreme Śiva beyond the fourth state (turyātīta),
which has the dual form of Nāda and Bindu, the triple form of Vāk, and arises from the fifth.
Kuṭilī is the radiant Lord Īśāna, who possesses earrings;
he is the limit of Rudra’s realization, consisting of the nature of will, knowledge, and action. || 125 ||
The atomic (āṇava), that which is caused by Māyā (māyaya), the unconditioned (akāmya), the sinful (pāpe), and the fivefold concealment (tirobhava);
the gross, the subtle, the great, the vital breath (prāṇa), and the manifest—these are the five coverings (kañcukas). || 126 ||
In the thirty [deities] such as Jīva and Icchā, there is the cause consisting of the thirty-six principles;
having made that which resides in the root the cause, it arises from Māyā-kuṇḍalinī.
I have declared the entire reality, which is the cause of creation and the soul of all;
that supreme power is inconceivable, while Māyā, when conceptualized, is the source of mental construction.
The inconceivable among the inconceivable, the witness, whose nature is the Self, higher than the highest,
consisting of all mantras, the Savior (Tāra), arisen as the Lord of the Enemy of the Savior (Tārariśva), and so forth. (129)
"Oṃ," it is said, is the form of light, residing within the form of light; it is Truth.
It is the binding of the *āsikā*, yet it is not the binding of the nose. (130)
For one who perceives "Om" itself, there is neither vehicle nor restriction;
this is the *Arthitattvasaṃgrahaviveka*.
The thirty-six principles (tattvas) consist of those beginning with Earth and ending with Kuṭilā. || 131 ||
By the will of Śiva, that which arises from Kuṭilā is the principle of Nāda, characterized by Pradhāna;
the Bindu, arisen in the midst of Nāda, is named after the purpose of Śiva and Śakti.
That which has arisen from knowledge and action is the very nature of Śiva and Śakti;
therefore, that reality which consists of knowledge and action is the essential nature of Sādākhya.
In Maheśa, knowledge is deficient and action is predominant; his form is that of the Tattvas.
In [the state of] Yoga, by the will [of Śiva], action is diminished as it is illuminated by Śuddhavidyā.
Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, Sādākhya, Bindu, and Nāda—these five are declared to be the Śiva-tattva; therein, the Bindu is the causal source.
Arising from the power of the *bindu*, it is *māyā*, the enchantress and cause of delusion;
it is formless, yet eternally abiding in a single form, pervading all things while its own nature remains unmanifested.
The emergence from Māyā is likewise threefold for the sake of the three types of action; that which is the destiny produced by time is karma, and that is well-determined.
Time, destiny, and the arisen individual soul—therein lies purification; something of will, action, and knowledge is manifested within one's own self. (138)
In its capacity as a cause, Vidyā likewise consists of the arising of manifold cognitions; for the sake of the immeasurable objects of passion, Vidyā is the sixth principle. (139)
Likewise, that which arises from the principles of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), its transformations (vikṛti), and the constituent powers (kalā),
as well as the state of being composed of the three qualities (triguṇatva) and the quality of time (kālaguṇatva), resides within primordial nature (prakṛti).
The sense-faculties grasp the subtle essence (*rasāna*) of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*);
likewise, the self (*ātman*), along with the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*), is grasped by the senses as objects through time. (141)

Māyā is that which is manifest; it is unmanifest, and that unmanifest is the Great One (Mahat). That which is beyond the elements is the principle (tattva); that is the mind, the instruments, and so forth.
And the quality of being a *guṇa* is likewise said to be threefold in its divisions. || 143 ||
The Taijasa destroys the Sāttvika, and likewise the Vaikharī destroys the Rājasa;
the Bhūtātiga destroys the Tāmasa; therefore, these three arms have arisen.
In the midst of that is the fiery ego (taijasāhaṃtā), and in its center arises the mental [ego] (mānasa);
it has the form of the instrument of knowledge (jñānakaraṇa) and originates from the Vaikharī-ego.
Sound and the rest constitute the fifth division, arising from the elements up to the ego-sense (ahaṃtā);
sound and the rest [also] exist within the five subtle elements (tanmātra), arising from ether (ākāśa) and the others. || 146 ||
From space, wind was produced; from wind, this mind-born [element] arose. From fire, water was produced; from water, the earth emerged. (147)
The square, the half-moon, the triangle, the hexagon,
and the circle are said to be the essential forms of earth and the other elements, arising from an intelligent cause.
Gold is white and reddish; black and smoky are the appearances of disease. || 149 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśa, and Īśāna are declared to be the cause; this world is said to be a differentiation of beings, and that [cause] is the source from which it arises. || 151 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as the fifth element;
and the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and the breath (nose) as the fifth sense organ. (152)
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ as the fifth. || 153 ||
Speech, movement, grasping, excretion, and the fifth, pleasure;
these, along with the other fifteen objects such as sound and so forth, constitute the twenty-five principles. 154.

The intellect (manas), the faculty of cognition (buddhi), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the mind (citta), and the knower of the field (jñetrajña) as the fifth—thus is the twenty-fifth principle, the Self (ātman), proclaimed. || 155 ||
Passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), and the deluding power (mohinī)—
this is declared as the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), celebrated as the sixth.
Śuddhavidyeśa, Sādākhya, and Śiva-Śakti as the fifth—this is declared to be the Śivatattva, which is both pure, impure, and mixed. (157)
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) extends to the heart; the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) extends to the space between the eyebrows;
the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) resides at the end of the crest-lock (śikhā); thus it is established that there is nothing beyond these principles.
All reality transcends the parts [of limited existence] and is the differentiation of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*).
In the *Jñānasiddhyāgama*, the second chapter, concerning the characteristics of Śiva, is completed.
The first [chapter] concerns the subject matter of the Tantra; the second concerns the characteristics of Śiva;
and [the third] concerns the attainment of grace regarding mantras and principles, arising from what is known as the descent of Śiva’s power.
Thus ends the discernment of the summary of the topics.
The Goddess said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, Śiva, wielder of the trident, Maheśvara!
Why has this group of beings been produced? Listen, O Goddess of beautiful countenance. (2)
The accomplishment of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning with Earth and ending with Śiva, [is performed] therein;
in the midst of that, for the sake of the reality of the Point (bindu), is the triangle arising from the qualities (guṇas). (3)
And by means of the tips of both [the hands], the threefold practice beginning with consciousness is performed;
through the drops, the enclosure, and the resonance, at that time, the three arise from the atoms.
In beginningless time, the threefold self arises from the manifestation of the differentiation of powers;
however, at the time of creation, each respective principle (tattva) comes into being.
The supreme power arises from the thirty-six subtle principles;
likewise, the power associated with poison is established within the self.
Then, that medicine ceases; therefore, it consists of the arising of knowledge. That arising of knowledge at that moment is the Śāmbhava state, which is union with Śiva.
Śiva has revealed the Time that arises from union with Śiva;
when Śiva abides as pure luminosity, he removes the darkness of the fetters of impurity.

For the sake of one's own self, the stainless self is brought about through the state of becoming stainless. According to the Śivadarśana: "The creation of the elements constitutes birth; the vision of awakening constitutes [true] existence. (9)
The body of the insentient, the atomic body, likewise the illusory body, the body of desire, and the body of the embodied one along with all [other] bodies. || 10 ||
The state of desiring liberation exists within the body of Śiva, while another remains situated in bondage;
from beginningless time, the crooked Kuṇḍalinī has remained as the threefold self.
In the aspect of differentiation, one should practice the state of the Bindu through the power of the Bindu (bindu-śakti).
At that time, the connection with impurity arises, and from that, its creation and so forth proceed.
The consciousness-self (vijñānātmā) is the fourth; the dissolution-self (pralayātmā) has three divisions;
and the totality-self (sakalātmā) likewise has three divisions; therefore, there are thirteen types [of selves]. || 13 ||

The Knower [perceives] the stainless Self as the Lord of Mantra-knowledge within ignorance; through knowledge, he perceives the new knowledge for the sake of dispelling the delusion of meaning, which arises from the stainless dissolution. (14)
The dissolution-ocean is consciousness; dissolution is the triad of the Sakala [states].
Bondage consists of the two types of bound consciousness, while liberation is the equanimous consciousness; the triad of the Sakala is thus established.
Thus, the threefold division of the self has been declared, as it was taught of old:
the Sakalātman, the Antarātman, the Jīvātman, and the Paramātman. (16)
The elemental self (bhūtātman), the quality-self (guṇātman), the mental self (manyatman) is recorded as the seventh;
the universal self (sarvātman) is declared through the distinctions of karma, and the embodied state is said to arise from the net of existents.
Likewise, Śiva, Śakti, and Līlā arise from the essence of the principles (tattva) in the center;
[he is] beyond the womb, higher than the highest.
The Power (Śakti) who is higher than the highest is devoted to Him; Sambhu is endowed with all [powers] and is beneficial.
Vijñāna, Mantra, Vidyeśa, Pradhāna, and Anta—these are the first seven, with Aṣṭama as the eighth.
Ananta, Sūkṣmaka, and likewise Mantri, Netra, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Śrīkhaṇḍin, and Śikhaṇḍin—these are the ones spoken of by Śiva. (20)
Thus, the fierce form with three eyes of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyā-Īśvaras),
proclaimed by the eight Lords of Knowledge, consists of seventy million great mantras.
The great mantra of seventy million, the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), consisting of seventy million [syllables],
[is] Māyā, Devāṇava... [and so forth].
Krodheśa, Maṇḍaleśa, Vīrabhadra, Kapālī, and so forth—endowed with such distinctions, this state of Rudra is like the water at the time of dissolution. (24)
Then, [he beheld] all that was described as distinct— the hosts of men and gods, the asuras, the Ādityas, the spirits (bhūtas), and so forth— arranged in successive order.
Thus, the division of the threefold self has been stated; the nine principles are not the cause.
The division of the Lord of Consciousness (Vijñāneśvara) is stated as five: Pralaya, Sāda, and Ākhyā as the fifth.
Maheśa, Rudra, and Viṣṇu, as well as the nine supreme forms of Brahmā; [then] Icchā, Jñānā, Kriyā, Māyā, Parā, Aindavī, and Tārakā.

The crooked ones (*kuṭilāḥ*) and the coiled ones (*kuṇḍalī*) are the nine primary powers (*prādhānyaśaktayaḥ*). The ninth is the primary [power], which is the cause of the two bonds (*bandha*). || 28 ||
Impurity (mala) has a nature distinct from power (śakti), because it arises from the three causes;
[it is so called] because it pierces the purpose of the "twisted" (kuṇḍalī) conflict. || 29 ||
These states are beginningless; they say that these are the very ornaments of the noose. || 30 ||
In the Āṇava and other [traditions], these five are said to be the piercing (vedha) and the connection (sambandha).
Therein, the fourfold divisions beginning with the Āṇava exist, and within them, Nārāyaṇa is established as the division.
O Rudra, the connection with the individual soul (*āṇava*) and so forth is described;
and this threefold division beginning with the individual soul is called the bond (*pāśa*) of Maheśvara. || 32 ||
The relationship between Āṇava and Vaiśāna...
[the principle of Śiva at the end of Āṇava], which consists of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā. (33)
The individual (āṇava) [power] is joined with the preceding ones; thereafter, it is deficient in the practitioner.
Thus, the stainless form of the Guru is said to be Śiva-śakti.
That reality is stainless and vast. || 34 ||
It is empty; it is the cause of the threefold self and its objects, characterized by the connection between the impure and the pure. || 35 ||
Due to the connection with beginningless impurity (mala), the individual soul (aṇu) is said to be possessed of limited knowledge;
due to being freed from beginningless impurity, the other is omniscient; therefore, He is Śiva. || 36 ||
The twenty-fourth principle is the Self (ātman), for which Brahmā is the presiding deity;
one should know that the twenty-seventh is Puruṣa, for which Viṣṇu is the presiding deity.
For the Rudras who have attained pure knowledge, [the worship is] of Kārtavīryeśa Maheśvara;
for those in the Sādākhya state, it is Īśānakartṛ, whose agent is that which arises from Nāda and Bindu.

Thus Śiva and Śakti have been described; from those two principles (tattva), this has arisen. Endowed with the characteristics of the universal self (sarvātman), the bound soul (paśu) remains in the state of bondage by the fetters (pāśabandha).
Māyā, which causes delusion and fainting, is situated within the three [principles].
The pure Self, which is self-luminous, is described as being divided into the pure and the absolute;
these four states constitute the fourfold Self, each of which is self-luminous. (40)
The gross [form] consists of five for the purpose of the fivefold acts; the subtle consists of five for the purpose of the fivefold acts.
For the sake of the fivefold acts upon those to be graced, it has fifteen parts as its function;
the gross form residing in the Sakala-self is for the purpose of the acts, while the subtle is known for the dissolution.
The five states beginning with waking and dreaming are the objects to be favored, having the nature of ritual action;
for the sake of attaining the samādhi of the pure self, they are conceived as the "state of the Self. (42)
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) should be performed through five stages. || 43 ||
The dissolution of consciousness, along with everything else, occurs through the pure atoms (śuddhāṇu);
that state should be brought about by means of the solitary and all-encompassing impurity (sakala-mala).
The states that have arisen from beginningless time are solely the cause of the void;
the state arising at the time of creation is Māyā, which possesses all [the powers] of consciousness. (45)
The state arising at the time of liberation remains beyond the waking state.
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, what is called 'bondage of the self'? (46)
The Lord said: Because of the defect of beginningless impurity, the Self undergoes bondage in three ways.
[For one who knows: "The embodied being is like the body; where is there no ignorance? (47)
Why is this beginningless and firm bondage, consisting of the defect of pure non-consciousness, [not removed]?
Like a beast bound by a strong rope, one is fettered by the notion that "this is copper" when it is actually brass, or "this is a human" when it is a ghost. (48)
There are those with three impurities (mala), those with two, and those with one; then there is the stainless self (nirmalātman) arising from the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Now, the beginningless impurity (anādimala) of men is proclaimed as their state of bondage (paśutva).
The husk is to be understood as the shell of the sprout of the seed of illusion;
when the ripening of the impurity occurs at its own time, it is accompanied by the ripening of merit.
In that state of mere [consciousness], for the sake of the power of knowledge, there arises the object which is its own self;
within that knowledge, by one's own will, [comes] death and the salutation of the Guru.
Through the mere compassion of the Guru, success and liberation shall come to human beings.
Thus concludes the third chapter, concerning the characteristics of the Self, in the *Jñānasiddhyāgama*.
The Goddess said: "O Maheśa, O Supreme Lord, what is this called 'pāśa'? The Lord said:
The noose, which consists of the bondage of the five impurities, is by nature a binding; it belongs to that which is previously described as absolutely indestructible and immutable. (2)
O Sage, even though there is a conjunction with Maheśvara, who is all-pervading,
this [individual soul] is powerless; therefore, due to his own lack of capacity, he has no agency over action.
The autonomy of the power of consciousness, obstructed by the state of being an animal (paśutva), has not been purified;
therefore, it depends upon the body of a living being devoid of the consciousness of action. || 4 ||
From the realm of Māyā down to the earth, along the path of the elements and the self, a person who is solely intent on enjoyment does not experience the pleasures situated therein. || 5 ||

The enjoyer of experience [performs] all actions; the supreme [reality] consists of the power of the fetters (*pāśa-śakti*). At the end, there arises an emergence that is distinct from that [power]. Make the bondage of the impurities (*mala*), such as the individual (*āṇava*) and others, abide solely in isolation.
It is solely the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), pure, and likewise the source of purity;
it is the connection with the impurity of Māyā, arisen from the self in the state of the Fourth (turya).
Who is bound? In what state? The state of deep sleep is one's own mental construction;
this state of dreaming is an illusion that conceals the possibility of the waking state.
This is the fifth impurity-state, imagined by one who is deluded regarding his own nature;
it is the connection between the Fourth Self and the vital breath, [whereas] in deep sleep there is no vital breath... || 9 ||

Sound and the rest, as well as speech and the rest, along with the ten beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the five organs of action beginning with the mind (*manas*), and the objects of the dream state— these constitute twenty-five.
These twenty-five consist of speech and the rest, beginning with the ear;
when these thirty have arisen, one should designate that as the waking state.
The five states beginning with waking— gross, subtle, very subtle, extremely subtle,
and the great-subtle— thus constitute the fivefold characteristic.

The state of yoga and the state of impurity are designated as two distinct types; thus established, bondage arises through the ends of bondage, while the possibility of liberation exists [within them]. 13.
This conceptualization of "bondage and liberation" is set in motion by the fetters of the bound souls (*paśu*).
Thus ends the fourth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the fetters (*pāśa-lakṣaṇa*), in the *Jñānasiddhyāgama*.
The Goddess said: O Lord of the Universe, for the sake of the peace of the world that has arisen from the Supreme Śiva,
what indeed is the purpose of the various states (avasthās) that have been proclaimed, as well as their recitation?
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess Maheśānī; [this is] the discourse concerning Śāmbhavī and likewise Śāṅkarī, which describes the distinctions of states through various connections.
The previously mentioned five states of the innate (sahaja) are proclaimed as follows:
waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth state (turya), and the fifth, which is beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 3 ||
The throat, the heart, the navel, and the root—these are the five locations; there is no fifth.
One proceeds through each station one by one; there is no self-consciousness [independent of them].
The states of abiding in the reality of the self are fivefold; the supports are fivefold;
the states of the fourteen sense organs are fivefold, eightfold, and fivefold.
Established in the senses, there are five [categories] such as *pañcaka* and so forth; the threefold divisions beginning with *mohikā*, and the fifth is the state of the path (*adhvāvastha*).
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state—these four states are internal distinctions; yet, transcending waking, they possess a single, uniform nature.
The third [state] is connected with qualities; it has five stages and one division.
That which is liberated from all stages is the supreme Śiva, beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
The twenty-five [principles] abide in the waking state through the objects of the organs of knowledge and action;
sound and the rest, as well as speech and the rest, arise from compassion in the dream state.
Likewise, in the middle [of the fourteen], there are the four states beginning with waking and ending with deep sleep;
by establishing the ego within the mind, the state of the Fourth (turya) is conceived. || 10 ||

The dissolution of the fluctuations of the mind is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); thus, the fifth [state] is indeed the reality of the Self, which is described as having such characteristics. || 11 ||
(35) That which is pervaded by the mind, beginning with sound and ending with speech, is the waking state;
the state of dream is prescribed as the extreme functioning of the internal organ. || 12 ||
The ego (ahantā) is of the nature of consciousness; it is the state beyond the fourth (aturoyaka), consisting merely of the latent impressions of consciousness.
O Citta, it remains established as that which has transcended what was done by Kṛṣṇa, being positioned within the instruments [of perception]. || 13 ||
Sound and the nature of touch, [and so forth]...
the states of the mind, bad dreams, and the principles are known through the intellect in the state of deep sleep.
The "I-ness" (ahantā) is merged in the fourth state (turya); these are the eight great waters. 15.
Sound and the rest constitute the fifth [state], waking; sound and the rest constitute dreaming;
the triad beginning with sound constitutes deep sleep; and sound and the rest constitute the second [state].
Likewise, the reality of the fifth sense organ is void of sound and the other [objects].
It is described as having three divisions beginning with the "pure" (kevala): the pure, the complete, and the impure. || 17 ||
One who is insentient, devoid of reality, devoid of *kalā*, and devoid of action is not a Tantrika;
likewise, one devoid of will and knowledge possesses only these characteristics [of being a non-Tantrika]. 18.
It encompasses all states and their various divisions, the cause for the connection with reality,
attained through the differentiation of forms and the senses, and arising from the three types of agents.
It is born from every womb and stands as the sprout of all karma. || 20 ||
Thus, this connection of characteristics, imagined as the entire self, [is manifested] through hells, heavens, and the worlds of men. || 21 ||
Likewise, the syllable Kāra is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), the body of the Knowledge-Acharya. || 22 ||
Merely through the exercise of compassion, the state of Śubhra is revealed;
it is beyond the waking state, supremely pure, and established in the state of liberation. 23.
At the time of mastery over that connection, the liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is revealed;
it arises from the threefold division beginning with the "isolated" (kevala), as stated in the three [sections]. 24.
Delusion, fainting, and illusion—[these are] the [obstacles];
the distinctions of the states of yoga have been declared... || 25 ||

The arising from the foundation established by the previously mentioned fivefold conduct is the state of the differentiation of reality; the domain [of this] consists of the waking state and so forth. (26)

The waking state is that which is thought of as other; the dream state is the end of reality; the deep sleep state is that from which consciousness arises; and the fourth state (turya) is that which is beyond the fourth, praised by the wise.
Uttering that which illuminates the state of deep sleep as the object of the waking state. 28.
That slight manifestation is the state of dreaming; existence is [the waking state]. That which is the fourth (turya) and the waking faculty, being empty, is the dream—the dissolution of causes.
Likewise, the fourth is deep sleep, which is Māyā... || 30 ||

The distinctions established in the final state [are such that] the connection is its quality; the triple activity of darkness is like a dream. That which is connected to the qualities is the void, yet it is the illuminator of reality. (32)
Having made this distinction between the states, the means for achieving mastery over them is yoga.
The waking and dreaming states are two-fold, while the fifth state, beginning with Māyā, is the victory. || 33 ||
Through the yoga of dhyāna, one attains victory; through sleep, the state of tamisraka;
through samādhi, the fourth (turya) victory;
[and] one should effect the victory of that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
The supreme reality is beyond the fourth state; it is beyond the fourth, the highest of the high.
The pure state is one; other than that, it arises from another life and from another source.
The chapter on the five states is completed.
The Goddess said: O Śiva, Īśa, Rudra, Īśāna, Mahādeva, Maheśvara!
What is called the fifth state, the division that is the bondage of the self? || 1 ||
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, listen; the states have been declared as limited.
[There are] one hundred and eight states... || 2 ||
The distinction of states is the differentiation of locations.
The Kevala, Sakala, and Śuddhāvasthāya are the three types of deluders;
furthermore, there are the Cāturthaka, Turya, Jāgrātīta, and Svapnaka. (3)
The fourth state (turya), the peak (jāgra), and that which transcends it (atīta), as well as the fourth state of waking (jāgrat-turya) which is easily awakened;
there are one hundred and eight states, with ten additional pure states, three divisions of the supreme state (parāvasthā), and sixteen intermediate states. || 4 ||
The causes are fivefold; having established the substratum of the fifth state, the causes for the connection with the qualities are fivefold. || 5 ||
The state of Māyā, Mahāmūrchā, Samanā, and likewise Unmanā—up to the end of Samanā is the net of bonds; at the end of Unmanā is Paraśiva.
The state of Śiva, the supreme state, and the state of the Self is the third. || 7 ||
The eightfold city, the four states, the intensely fierce, the risen, and the sleeping; the threefold visions, the balanced state, and the meditative absorptions. (8)
The Unmanifest is the supreme Manifest; it is devoid of the male and female genders. || 9 ||
The specific description of all states is divided into five stages;

likewise, according to the previously mentioned method, the twenty-fifth [principle] among the five is established as the womb of the state of the Great Yogin, which is the void of all things (sarvaśūnya). || 11 ||
The state of being (bhūtāvasthā) and the state of impurity (malāvasthā) consist of the two groups of five—the gross and the subtle. || 12 ||
Freed from all states, it is the very nature of the Self;
freed from all states, it is the supreme Śiva, beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 13 ||
The supreme reality beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is the essence of all realities; thus,
it is one alone, supportless, the single state of being beyond mind (unmanī).
It is liberated from all states and devoid of all thought. || 15 ||
By means of which the Śiva-yogin remains established in the seal of silence (maunamudrā), so too does he become [one with that state];
the conventional reality of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings. (16)
This is the specific distinction for yogins regarding the relationship [of the deities]:
one should sequentially place the pure eight limbs of yoga, which grant victory in all states, within the *sthāpanā* and *āsana*.
The supreme Śiva is beyond all states and transcends even reality;
thus ends the section on the distinctions of states.
The Goddess said: O Lord, supreme over all principles, for the sake of illuminating the reality of knowledge,
[please explain] the differentiation of knowledge, the qualities of knowledge, the nature of knowledge, and that which arises from it.

What is said regarding the tenfold classification of the characteristics of the teacher of knowledge and the non-teacher, as well as the disciple and the non-disciple; and the determination of knowledge and the meaning of reality? (19)

Śaṅkara said: "The knowledge of sound, the reality, the various systems of doctrine, and even pure consciousness— these exist within Śaivism according to the authority of the divisions of Śaiva tradition."
From evil comes evil knowledge, which takes the form of heretical (pāṣaṇḍa) knowledge;
both this stained and stainless higher cognition (vijñāna) are equal.
The Śāmbhava knowledge, the conventions, the hearing of the Siddhāntas, as well as the Nigrantha, the Jñānin, and the Mūḍha—these are the various divisions of the Sāṃkhya. (22)
Conceptualization and discursive thought are purified by awakening;
through the distinction between light and non-light, there are eight [types of] mental constructions.
The fallacious characteristics of word and meaning, as well as the particular characteristic known through words, do not lead to the knowledge of reality;
rather, it is the immeasurable practice of reality that initiates the knowledge of reality. (24)
p.
39) By one who knows the meaning of the various fragments of the *samayas*, [is known] the characteristic of the *samaya*.
— *Samayaviveka*—
The Śaiva, the Śivādvaita, and the dualistic Śivasammelana—these are three;
the fourth extends up to the Pāśupata, while the fifth is the Mahāvrata.
The sixth is indeed the Kālāmukha, and the seventh is likewise the Bhairava.
The eighth is for the purpose of piercing the left; it should be equal... || 27 ||
Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Bauddha, Māṣañcaka, as well as Lokāyata, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā, and Vaiṣṇava; || 28 ||
Thus, there are eight external divisions and sixteen internal ones;
this knowledge, which consists of both difference and non-difference, is primarily characterized by the doctrine of Māyā.
He who is the sun for the darkness of logic, the master of mantras, yantras, and tantras;
who abides in bliss, who is peaceful, who has transcended peace, and who is higher than the highest.
Prārabdha-karma and the feet, along with the other proponents of medicinal herbs—
this is declared to have eight parts, [and] twenty-four.
