The sacred scriptures (tīrtha-śāstra) and the authoritative means (pramāṇa), the fifth being the purpose of worship (arcanādhyārtha);
the distinctions between the external and internal [worship], and the sixfold divisions of ritual intentions (saṃkalpa). || 32 ||
Now, there are four types of hermitages, and likewise sixteen;
[the views are] those who speak like Brahmā, those who speak like Vāda, those who speak of reality (tattva), and those who speak of emptiness (śūnyaka).
Thus, the twenty-eightfold division arising from the five Śivas, produced by the Śrutis, Āgamas, and Tantras, originates from the Māyā-kuṇḍalinī.
The realization of the truth of Vedānta is its means;
the knowledge of the consensus regarding the meaning of the Vedas—that knowledge is the supreme state. (35)
The distinctions between the threefold and twofold [divisions] are correctly initiated by knowledge;
the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) constitute that which exists as a duality.
The vision of Vedānta reveals the repose of the beloved within one's own essential nature—
Brahman, whose form is truth, consciousness, and infinity, and who is infinite. (37)
Established in bliss, peaceful, transcending peace, higher than the highest,
it is the source of all that arises from the conceptualizations of various scriptures.

Having seen that the various meanings of the scriptures possess a single underlying meaning, one should remain established in that fragmentary [unity]. The practice of the sixty-four arts and the discerning knowledge of those arts [are required]. (39)
The practice of the eightfold yoga, other forms of yoga, and the various births;
the contemplation of the conscious and the unconscious, and knowledge—these exist as manifest and unmanifest states.
The liberation of the heretics is established in the state of stone, a mere conceptualization of knowledge. (41)

I am His servant, who has taken refuge in Him—He who is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), both pure and impure, and whose knowledge manifests as dual, non-dual, and so forth. || 42 ||
The mixed [tradition] is twofold: the Śāmbhava, which is the knowledge of fear associated with Śambhu;
and the Pāśupata, which is the vision of the established tenets of knowledge for the purpose of transcending the bonds of the Lord of Bonds. (43)
The secret knowledge and so forth are concealed; the root knowledge and so forth are delusive.
There are many divisions of Sāṃkhya, which are twofold: pertaining to primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti).
The Puruṣa-sāṃkhya is the fourth, while the Sura-sāṃkhya is the fifth; Nirīśa is the fifth [variant], and Yogasāṃkhya is the sixth.
This Sāṃkhya is distinct; it is established as the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
It is volition, imagination, knowledge, conceptualization, its own activity, and pride. (46)
Awakening is the self-nature, abiding in luminosity; awakening is the vision of space.
Luminosity is innate to the three worlds; luminosity is captivating to the mind. (47)

The knowledge of the noose is indeed the binding of the bound soul; such is the locus for the arising of knowledge.
(41) *Ācāryalakṣaṇaviveka*.
O Maheśvara, being composed, I shall describe the characteristics of the teacher (*ācārya*).
He was of the same caste as his father, possessed of knowledge, self-controlled, truthful, and devoted to compassion.
It contains the meaning of the investigations into various scriptures and the vision of various philosophical systems;

The teacher of knowledge and action is the lord who is superior through the four initiations.
The distinction of the characteristics of one who is not a teacher.
Desire, anger, pride, greed, delusion, and envy arise from them; as do egoism, conceptual constructions, and the threefold conjunctions.
One who has not practiced various scriptures, nor practiced various yogas;

Lack of practice regarding the knowledge of reality, being devoid of self-knowledge, lack of practice regarding the knowledge of Śiva, and treachery toward Śiva—[these are the obstacles]. (9)
Lack of trust and excessive cruelty are the characteristics of one who is deluded.
This is the discernment of the characteristics of a true disciple.

Discernment regarding unworthy disciples.

cruel, and full of conceptual constructions— such as one whose big toe grows [abnormally] and so forth.
One who is ill-behaved, characterized by wicked conduct, foul speech, a troubled mind,
and a harsh countenance— such qualities are possible in one who is corrupt.

He thoroughly protects the domain consisting of those who commit treason against the Guru, treason against Śiva, treason against the scriptures and their own tradition, and treason against the lineage.
Characterized by such qualities as these is the mark of one who is immoral and indolent.
The Discrimination of the Determination of Knowledge.
The knowledge of the fetter, the knowledge of the bound soul, and the knowledge of the Lord—these three are supreme.
Satyabhānu, Bhava, and Jñāna—thus [are] the eight [deities] beginning with Jñānottama.
That would be established within the established doctrine of that Vedānta.
Knowledge is said to be twofold: the higher is known as that which transcends speech, and the other is called awakening; this supreme scripture is the most excellent.
The chapter on the characteristics and forms of knowledge is completed.
The Goddess said: O Śivānanda, Lord of the World, Śivayogin, Maheśvara!
[Grant] initiation for the sake of discerning the true meaning of right conduct.
The established doctrine of the pure Śaiva is the domain of Vedāntic knowledge;
it consists of the two conventions of difference and non-difference, which serves as an entrance to pure gnosis.
The Supreme Guru is the pure path of union, the impeller of both the pure and the impure, the destroyer of the bonds of the bound soul (paśu), and the embodiment of yoga and knowledge.
The definitive conclusion of that which is more secret than the secret consists of twelve divisions;
the specific characteristics of how each of these should be practiced are now being stated.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Great Goddess, to this question which summarizes all matters;
likewise, hear the true meaning of the twelve questions, which is more secret than the secret.
The good teacher, the spiritual preceptor, and the master—therein is a threefold conceptualization:
the teacher for the sake of instruction in childhood, while the mantra, the tantra, and the wealth constitute the spiritual preceptor.
The sequence of instruction is as follows: its master is prescribed [as threefold], namely the other, the divine, and the accomplished; thus the Guru is of three kinds according to the means.
Divine mental awakening is beneficial for one's own Śiva-nature;
it is the perfected vision of the distinction [between them], established through the scriptures and the passage of time.
At the end of the period for his livelihood, the attendants prepared cooked food that was auspicious for him;
then, for the sake of his own initiation, the teacher acted as the awakener.

The dissolution of consciousness, as well as all those who hold authority over the three worlds, the supreme skull of Śiva, the bindu, and the conceptualizations of knowledge— [all these are contained therein].
The threefold nature arising from consciousness consists of the inseparable union of the signified and the signifier;
thus, the disciple is threefold, the teacher is threefold, and this threefold state arises from such awakening.
Thus, the true teacher is one whose purpose is accomplished, who promotes right conduct,
who possesses perfect awakening, who is joined with the true guru, and who is born from the essence of eternal bliss.
Thus ends the *Ācāryaviveka*.
There are four-footed conceptualizations of various systems:
the animal [sacrifice], the Vedic initiation, the Śaiva, and my own.
Many disciples of Śambhu who were initiated into other tantras,
such as Aṣṭapāda and others, [attained] knowledge through their own initiation.
Initiation for the sake of the eight siddhis consists of eight types, distinguished by their superior qualities;
such are the conceptualizations regarding these various divisions within the world.
Having established the sixfold Śaiva cause— consisting of Samaya, Viśeṣa, Nirvāṇa, and likewise Śāmbhava— seated upon the consecrations (abhiṣeka).
Knowledge, yoga, and ritual action—these three constitute the previously mentioned group of six.
For the purpose of distinguishing the various paths of attainment, those who have been initiated by their own [guru] perceive these manifoldly.
The visual initiation, the tactile initiation, the verbal initiation, and likewise the mental initiation;
furthermore, the initiation of yoga in the scripture—alas, it is manifold.
Knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
it is bestowed and destroyed—thus is the term "initiation" (dīkṣā) used here.

Therefore, for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its state of bondage and the fivefold impurities (malapañcaka), the rite of initiation (dīkṣā)—which effects the unification of that individual soul with Śiva—must be performed. What is called the "division of Śaivism" is simply the established doctrine (siddhānta) of the pure Śaivas. What else could it be?
The Śaiva [tradition] is threefold: the beginningless (anādi), the beginning (ādi), and the mixed (miśra).
The Guru-Śaiva is the fourth, and the fifth is the internal division.
The Mahāśaiva is the sixth division, while the Bheda-śaiva is the seventh.
One should know Abheda-śaiva as the ninth, likewise Yoga-śaiva;
one should know Jñāna-śaiva as the tenth, and Ūrdhva-śaiva as the eleventh.
Indeed, the twelfth is Ājñā-śaiva, while the thirteenth is Nandī-śaiva;
on the fourteenth day is Artha-śaiva, and [on the fifteenth] is Tattva-śaiva.
The sixteenth is the Śuddhaśaiva; thus stands the classification of the Śaiva systems.
This is the determination of the meaning of the Śaiva divisions, consisting of the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati).
The Vedānta, the Śaiva Siddhānta, the Yogānta, the Nādāntaka,
and the Bodhānta— therein lies the fivefold end, the pure Śaiva Sudarśana.
Established therein, it is peaceful, pure, and the initiator of Śaivism.
The Śaivaviveka is completed.
Now listen to the Vedānta, the very essence of all scriptures:
the individual self and the supreme self—the oneness of these two.

Truth, knowledge, infinity, and bliss constitute its essential nature; it is revealed in a single sentence that gives rise to many scriptures, yet it is not something that can be fully manifested [by words].
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas are established as arising from the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa);
however, the Vedānta consists of great statements (mahāvākya) that reveal the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta).
The Purāṇa is the Bhārata scripture, which possesses the nature of reality through its traditional expositions.
The science of mantras, the science of narratives, and the science of ritual offerings are delusive;
whereas the Vedānta, the Śaivasiddhānta, and the Śiva-śāstra grant the liberation of the perfected ones.
Having placed that Great Saying upon his head and having placed the feet of the Three-eyed One at his three places,
he was born with a variegated body possessing three eyes and arising from the three characteristics.
The threefold waking, the threefold dreaming, the threefold deep sleep, and the threefold fourth state—
this is the Self, whose nature is the light of consciousness, consisting of three steps and the meaning of those three steps.
Endowed with such characteristics as these, the metaphor "That art thou" (tat tvam asi) takes the form of the nectar of awakening; it is the domain that transcends conventional observances (samaya).
The syllables A, U, and M are the three parts of the Praṇava;
the oneness of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is characterized by the three feet, each possessing a hundred thousand characteristics.
Within that, Śabalā possesses a limited differentiation, of which the sixteenth is supreme; it is the soul, beyond words, liberation, and all-pervasive—such is its characteristic therein.
The waking state of the self, the waking state of the other, and the waking state of Śiva—this is the triple waking state.
The dreaming state of the self, the dreaming state of the other, and the dreaming state of Śiva—this is the triple dreaming state.
The sleep of the self (ātma-supti), the supreme sleep (para-supti), and the sleep of Śiva (śiva-supta) constitute the triple sleep (trisuptaka).
The fourth state of the self (ātma-turya), the supreme fourth (para-turya), and the fourth state of Śiva (śiva-turya) constitute the triple-fourth (trituryaka).
Thus, divided twelvefold, these are proclaimed as the ten states.
Be awake in the waking state, awake in the dreaming state, and awake in the third state, deep sleep;
be awake in the fourth state, the Turiya, and at that very moment, awake in the supreme fifth state.
The sixth is indeed Paravyoma, while the seventh is Parāvasthā;
the eighth is Viśvagrāsa, and the ninth is likewise Upaśānta.
Śiva has created ten [states], namely the ten states of speech;
the word *tvam* and the word *tat* are twofold, while the words *asit* and *traidha* are threefold.

Those who possess the threefold purpose—namely, for their own sake, for the sake of others, and for the sake of Śiva—have declared their own universe to be radiant; O Knower, these are the third state in its threefold division.
Ādiśakti, Parāśakti, and Śivaśakti are the three powers;
this [work] is endowed with their characteristics and follows the sequence of injunctions for the meaning of Vedānta.
(Life-liberation, liberation after death, and liberation as Śiva are the third;
this is the discernment of difference and non-difference.)
I am Śiva—this is the established conclusion; "That I am"—this is the end of the Vedas.
Having grasped the essence of the meaning of the Vedas, I have proclaimed this path arising from the ninefold principles.
Therefore, having attained the true knowledge of Vedānta and the Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy,
the individual soul (aṇu), situated within Māyā-kuṇḍalinī, becomes divided into two.
It is the absolute awakening within the Self, the self-luminous nature of the individual soul;
it is the perfect awakening of the fourth state (turiya) during waking, the very essence of the Self according to the Upanishads.
Likewise, one should know the distinction of states, the gift that transcends impurity, one's own self,
the two-fold division of the Vedas and Āgamas, and the distinct nature of the Self.
Indeed, the relationship between the distinct and the non-distinct is the essential nature consisting of consciousness;
that which abides in the essential nature of the Self is non-distinct, while that which is called *prakṛti* is said to be distinct.
Therein is the exposition of the meaning of the sentence, the meaning of the syllable *praṇava*, and the meaning of the *mudrā*;
having awakened the purpose of the experience of bathing, it is the entry into pure knowledge.
For the purpose of illuminating pure knowledge, it arises as pure *sāyujya*;
for the purpose of conceptualizing the three principles (*tattva*), it is the twofold mixture of pure and impure.
For the sake of awakening to the meaning of Vedānta and for illuminating one's own direct experience,
he therefore revealed the nature of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), which liberates both the individual soul and its bonds.
The eight-rayed [sun] is indeed the union of the two—the knowledge of yoga and its culmination in the compendium;
it is liberated from all states, the form of the Guru, higher than the highest.
O Śaṅkarī, that which is secret is the Śāmbhava; its threefold nature is more secret than the secret, the supreme of the Guru, and the investigation of the twelve topics previously mentioned.
The Chapter on the Means of Attraction is completed.

The ninth chapter: On the Established Doctrine.
Therefore, initiation is tenfold according to the sequence of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), and the Lord (pati):

The third is for the sake of purifying reality; the fourth is the form of the self;
the fifth is clarity, and the sixth is the purification of the self.
The reality of all things consists of four divisions arising from Māyā and Kuṇḍalinī;
specifically, one should perform one's own duty regarding the three previously mentioned realities.
In that [state], the realization of the true nature consists of the vision and cultivation of reality;
make it so that the purification of reality exists as a distinct form, while the state of karma remains empty of reality.
Formless, consisting of color and consciousness, its range extends to the limit of changelessness;
undivided yet appearing divided, that which is emptiness is the very nature of the self.
Whatever wisdom arises from the practice of yoga, that is not of the nature of atoms;
that form which pervades the mind is entirely self-luminous.
That space arises as the object; the purification of the self is its own state.
The void is twofold—formed and formless—and is the supreme Śiva beyond the fourth state.
That is the supreme reality, the immovable pillar, beyond all principles, the highest Śiva.
Now, the discernment of the vision of Śiva:
"Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self of this living being is placed within its secret cave."
Empty of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the self-luminous light within the center of the Self is the supreme experience of its own cognition.
The oneness of one's own self and the Supreme, the Yoga of Śiva arising from Śiva,
transcending the ten states through their union, is the reflective awareness of the supreme state.
Its own nature consists of qualities such as truth and so forth; it is purified by the definition of the Vedic statement;
it is truth-bliss, the great light, which brings about the experience of the enjoyment of Śiva.
The chapter on the Exposition of the Siddhānta is completed.

[Please explain] the effort for liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) for the sake of attaining the ten stages.

The Discernment of the Conduct of Initiation:

By bearing the venerable state upon one's head and through the contemplation that "I am He," there arises the liberation while living (jīvanmukti), the supreme liberation, and indeed the liberation of Śiva itself.
Having reflected, "I am Śiva," the knowledge of Śiva has been revealed;
the knowledge of Śiva is the supreme knowledge, realized as "I am He."
Thus, they say that I am the state born of the sacred revelation; I am the servant arising from the tradition (samaya).
"I am He" is the established conclusion—the pure end of purity, born of the individual soul.
The body is the manifest temple of the deity; the living soul is the god Sadāśiva himself.
One should discard the "offering-wreath" (nirmālya) of ignorance and worship with the thought, "I am He.
One should worship that which is established in its own nature through the initiation of knowledge and which reveals the power of knowledge.
For the purpose of illuminating the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), the power of darkness (*tamaḥ-śakti*) becomes distinct;
when the power of darkness becomes distinct, it reveals liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
For the purpose of illuminating liberation while living (jīvanmukti), one should remain established in supreme liberation.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, O Maheśāna, O Śaṅkara, O Compassionate One!
"I am Śiva"—having attained this, what further goal is there to be reached? What remains to be attained is the dawning of the state of Śambhu.
Īśvara said:
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, listen to the Śāmbhavī, the Śāṅkarī, and the Gaurī [mantras]. For the sake of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), the form of the Self has been revealed.
The body situated as the form of the elements is called the *svarūpa-deha* (essential body);
the subtle body situated as the *puryaṣṭaka* (eightfold city) is born from the three *prakṛtis*.
Thereafter, O Mohinī,
having cast off today this physical body born of the five sheaths, as well as the vital breath and the subtle body produced from the skin.
The body, composed of the five elements, is conceived as having the form of the constituent minerals:
lymph, blood, flesh, bone, fat, marrow, and semen.
Having abandoned the seven elements, one should abandon the sense of hearing;
the five beginning with speech should be abandoned, and one should abandon sound as the fifth.
Speech and the rest are the five to be abandoned; sound and the rest are the pentad of persons. Having relinquished all this, remain awake as the supreme state.

Having abandoned the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), one remains established as "waking-waking" (jāgraj-jāgra). Having abandoned the principle of knowledge, one becomes established as "dream-waking" (svapna-jāgra).
Having abandoned the Śiva-tattva, which arises from Māyā-mohinī,
the Puruṣa-tattva is the witness of the states of waking and sleep born thereof.
Having abandoned the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*), which arises solely from the past,
and [having abandoned] the arising of the impurity of separate existence through mere compassion of the Guru;
The state beyond the fourth (atiturya) exists for the sake of illumination as the very form of consciousness within the individual soul (jīva).
The states beginning with waking (jāgrat) and so forth remain concealed within the primordial ground;
from concealment, they emerge at the forefront of waking, and this waking state is the bestower of the fruits of enjoyment.
Waking becomes the desired sleep, while in the fourth state (turya), it is the deluding Jayā.
One should abandon that atomic bondage (āṇavabandha) which exists in the waking state, for it is detrimental to the self;
Brahmā resides in the waking-waking state, and Hari resides in the waking-dreaming state.
When Rudra is situated in the state of waking sleep, he is likewise deluded by darkness;
when a living being is situated in the Turya of the waking state, he perceives Sadāśiva as transcending the waking state.
His bondage consists of the purpose of the power of the Bindu, arising from that which is irreproachable.

The fourth state (turya) is likewise described as being the waking state; therein is the vision of the individual self (jīvātman), and the word "thou" (tvam-pada) arises from the nature of that fourth state.
The individual soul (jīvātman), free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and pure as the referent of the term "Thou" (tvaṃ-padārtha),
pervades all that— this entire world of moving and non-moving beings within the two bodies.
For the purpose of illuminating that which was not seen through awakening, and for the destruction of the perception of [phenomenal] existence,
the cultivation of all objects is proclaimed as the fourth self, the illuminator.

The refutation of consciousness is pervasive and reveals the state of being a bound animal (paśutva); that which is the light of consciousness arises from the fourth state (turya), while the portion of darkness arises from the waking state.
The union of these two is the conceptualization of the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).
The twenty-one states of the object of perception belong to the principle of the Puruṣa;
however, in the sense of the Jīva-Brahman, there is no abiding in a state of oneness within the three parts.
Therefore, the wise, being established in that Self which is both within themselves and in others, are free from doubt.
At that time, the other names are the cause of that state of being a bound soul (paśu).
That which is established through the absence of such [limited] cognition is situated as pure and absolute (śuddhakevala).
In the supreme ether is the true meaning of reality, which reveals liberation while living;
the Supreme Self is established as that very light of one's own consciousness.
The supreme state is indeed luminosity, whose range transcends all things;
it is Brahman, whose body is space, beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), the supreme Śiva.
The individual soul (jīvātman), having attained its true nature, whether minute or great, is proclaimed to reside within the cave of the heart;
for its sake and for that [supreme] purpose, there is that further, supreme state.
The supreme secret that swallows all, the auspicious source of the self of all,
endowed with all that exists, that void which is the birthplace of peace.

That which is established as auspicious, peaceful, beyond peace, and higher than the highest— O Knower of Tranquility, that is the attainment of the supreme means for the unification of the individual soul with the Supreme.
The Self and Paraśiva—these are the three categories;
the triple consciousness, when its distinctions have been dissolved, is the source of this [reality].
You are the bone in the fourth state, and the individual soul (jīva) within that; therein lies that which is higher than the highest in the fourth.
When the identity of the two has been attained, Śiva is both supreme and non-supreme;
O Śaṇa, He is threefold, consisting of the desirable, the beginningless, and so forth.
You study that; within it lies pure liberation through the self. For the sake of the purity of the self, that which is liberated is far superior to the highest of the high.
"You are this," "What is that? "That is you," and "That is his";
he who understands the meaning of these statements is one whose mind is purified by meditation.

The distinct, the non-distinct, and the both distinct and non-distinct—these three types have been proclaimed.
Because it is free from the state of being [conditioned], it is the form of one's own self within those who are like you;
O Śiva, it is supreme bliss, the experience of that which is tranquil, pure, and the assembly of the perfected ones (siddhas).
Your nature as the Self pervades the three states and remains established therein;
having attained the state of the threefold Self, you abide in the ninefold Self through its various divisions.
Indication is threefold: jahallakṣaṇā (indication with abandonment), ajahallakṣaṇā (indication without abandonment), and jahadajahallakṣaṇā (indication with both abandonment and non-abandonment).
The three steps are to be known as purity; likewise, the meaning of the three steps is purity.
Through the purity of the three steps, one should know that self-purification occurs within the meaning of the three steps.
"The beds cry out," "the cowherd station dwells on the Ganges"—
because [these are used] thus, it is said that the knower is not the cause of duality.
Standing in the midst of those men, let him proclaim: "Remain firm!
The Guru [is he] who, endowed with these specific qualities, abides within all bodies.

Therefore, having grasped with his speech that which is the most ignorant of men, the awakener [of others] acts according to his own karma; the embodied soul does not create the body, for he is the non-doer.

"The white one stands still, yet runs"—this is the meaning of the speed (*java*).

let this be the state of union (sāyujya) established as one with Paśupati.

for what person is there whose own vision is not pervaded by the mere distinction of the three times?
Thus, those three words are pure; they are spoken for the purpose of defining its characteristics:

Truth, knowledge, and the infinite; the infinite born of the Maruts;
the self-nature of truth, knowledge, auspiciousness, and bliss—these are the threefold qualities.
Bliss is the power; that which is attained from the supreme true guru should be applied.
In that regard, his own form and appearance consist of the manifestation of the three qualities;
and for the sake of its various modes, there is the perfection of qualities such as truthfulness and the rest.
Form, fragrance, quality, beauty, as well as arising and the blue lotus (*utpala*);
likewise, "and so forth" refers to its varieties, while its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is its arising (*udbhava*).
The three categories—knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—are subsumed within this;
therefore, its essential nature everywhere consists of the embodiment of light and bliss.
May they always meditate upon that supreme liberation, which arises from the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva); having attained it, one shall achieve union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
The determination of the statement: "Thou art That" (tattvamasi). "Thou art" is twofold; "That art thou" is threefold.

Having abandoned the state of being both cause and effect, one is distinguished as perfect consciousness (pūrṇabodha).
Full within, empty;
full without, full in the middle, free from affliction. Empty within, empty without, empty in the middle, free from affliction.
Refutation of the statement.
"That you, that I, that he; it is not, it is not, it is not, and it is not"—that which exists as "neither empty nor non-empty," [is the truth].

I alone have wandered in delusion; therefore, one should abandon these three.
One's own direct experience.

The "Mūkasvapna" [is] the knowledge of the Self, which is unsurpassed bliss; this is established through its traditional transmission (*sampradāya*). The section on the tradition concerning the reality of the light arising from peace is completed.

for the three worlds do not consist of sacrificial limbs, nor lotus limbs, nor wheel limbs.
The entire world is the limb of the Liṅga; therefore, the world belongs to Maheśvara.
The Liṅga is joined with arms, its right and left feet resting upon the Goddess’s lap, its base at the Gomukha, and its water-receptacle at the end of the foot;
situated in the middle of the womb, it is established as Sadāśiva, whose nature is beyond mind (manonmani).
Peaceful, seated in the lotus posture, wearing a crown of the moon, and five-faced;
[holding] a trident, a vajra, a sword, and an axe... [and so forth].
In his left hands, he holds a serpent, a noose, a varada-mudrā, fire, and a goad;
adorned with various ornaments and resembling a crystal gem, there is one known as Sādāśiva.
Five-faced and five-colored, consisting of the deities of the five directions,
possessing fifty eyes and endowed with ten hands and ten states.
Thus, the form known as Sādākhya is endowed with ten ears;
Sādākhya consists of five divisions, and all of it likewise originates from the Bindu.
The agent of action and his own form, which is the differentiator of the state called Sādākhya;
[the form] impelled by the portions of Śiva’s Sādākhya;
that which is like crystal is Īśāna, while the eastern face, which has the luster of saffron, is Tatpuruṣa.
The southern face is like collyrium and has a terrible countenance;
the northern face should be like a shimmering hibiscus flower;
the western face, however, is Sadyojāta, with a luster equal to cow’s milk.
Thus, accompanied by his own Manonmanī in the form of Sādākhyā, he [attains] Śiva;
[he perceives] Manonmanī as the central radiance among the eight powers beginning with Vāmā.
The supreme Śiva, who is beyond the mind (*unmana*), is to be known as possessing nine powers;
because of its connection with the mind and that which is beyond the mind, it is designated as "other than the mind" (*manonya*).
Within that very center is the means for attaining enjoyment.
In its center is that which leads to supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and perfections (*siddhi*); in its center is that which pierces through liberation;
in its center is the purpose of all forms; therefore, it is the cause everywhere.
Likewise, the *liṅga* consisting of the syllables *ha* and *u*, as well as the *liṅga* composed of all *liṅgas*.
The letter *ma* is declared to consist of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), being the primary *liṅgasūtra*;
it is the portion of the *suṣumnā*, as well as the path leading to the temple (*prāsāda*).
The Bindu is the seat (pīṭha), Śakti is the liṅga of Nāda, and likewise Śiva;
the syllable Om (praṇava) consists of equal parts of Bindu and Nāda.
The syllable *praṇava* is proclaimed as the imperishable; its crest-jewel consists of the *bindu* and *nāda* situated at the tip of the flame.
It has the form of the digits of *bindu* and *nāda*, embodying the nature of all mantras.
It is the differentiation of the digits of *bindu* and *nāda*, appearing in the form of the moon, the sun, and fire.
The form of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā consists of Will, Knowledge, and Action;
by piercing the Bindu, one reaches the triangular portion, the Egg, which is the very nature of the Tattvas.
The principles (tattvas) belonging to Rudra and Īśāna constitute the practice arising from the Bindu;
the triangle has the form of Tripurā, and it is the source of speech, action, and liberation.
In the midst of that is the Supreme Śakti; likewise, in the midst of that is Tripura, as well as Vāgbhava, Svarṇa, [and] the action of the whetstone.
The self is the liberated crystal; Tripura is the causal power (śakti). Abiding in the nature of the five forms, it possesses the nature of the five powers.
It is declared to be the five-fold impurity of the fetters (pāśa); this is the fifth, the pure reality of the principles (tattva).
The fivefold [reality] is known as the "mixed" (*saṃbhinnam*);
it is proclaimed by the injunctions of the Five Fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), consisting of the digits (*kalā*) of the pentad.
Having the form of the five activities, he is the cause of the fivefold functioning of speech.
Everything arising from the Bindu is permeated by the fifth syllable;
it is declared to be half, or six, or many, consisting entirely of the five Kalās.
Consciousness and the rest, whose nature is threefold, are the cause;
just as the ocean [is the cause] of the arising and dissolution of waves,
spray, and so forth, even so, within the form of the Bindu, there is the arising and dissolution of all principles (tattvas).
The power Khecarī, the power Bhūcarī, likewise the power Śaktidṛggocarī,
the power Vyomavāmeśvarī, and the fifth, arisen from the Bindu.
The levels of mantra consist of Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Parā, Dikcarī, Tādicarī, and Śakticarī.
Desire, knowledge, action, māyā, and the supreme (parā)—these are the five deities;
they consist of the essence of the syllables A, U, and M, along with the bindu, nāda, and kalā.
Everything arisen from the principle of the Bindu is manifested at the time of creation;
all that is within the principle of Kuṭilā.
Between the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, there arises the form of the *kuṇḍalinī*;
situated in the midst of the three *kuṇḍalinīs*, it is the nature of light, higher than the highest.
The body of this [deity] arises from the power of the Mātṛkās of its own phonemes;
the power of the Mātṛkās should be understood as the definitive meaning of all scriptures.
The syllable Oṃ is the imperishable Brahman, whose form is the Kalā, transcending even the Transcendent (Tara).
"Oṃ" is for the sake of awakening to all; "Oṃ" is the cause of all.
Regarding birth-impurity (*sūtaka*): when [a child] is born, there is impurity at the conclusion of the mantra that has arisen.
(72) There would be a fault in both cases, and all of that would become fruitless—
especially regarding all mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
The purification of mantras is proclaimed for the purpose of casting off [impurities].

The syllable *oṃ* is the letter of knowledge (*jñāna-varṇa*), while other letters are of the nature of action (*karma-rūpaka*). Therefore, this supreme awakening is the illuminator of the *paramātman*.
The root, the middle, and the subtle—these are the threefold distinctions of the *tāra*.
It is connected with the five *praṇavas* and consists of the digits (*kalā*) of the five principles (*tatvas*).
The five principles arise from the five syllables through their divisions of kalās;
beginning with the Praṇava and ending with the letter Ya, they consist of five or six syllables.
Uttering the six-syllabled mantra joined with the five-syllabled *praṇava*, she intends for absorption into that [mantra],
because the six paths exist within the uttered six-syllabled mantra.
The division of the paths of the six stages is the sequence of ritual procedures for the Kriyā-Śaivas;
perform likewise that which is to be enjoyed by those who follow the difficult path for the sake of their own actions.
The meaning of "time" (adhvan) is that at whatever time [it occurs], there is the destruction of karma;
[this applies to] the division of phonemes (varṇa), parts (kalā), principles (tattva), mantras, and indeed the worlds (bhuvana).
The dissolution of the signified and the signifier is to be grasped through the three islands;
that form of the signified and the signifier arises from the states of Śiva and Śakti.
The state of Śiva pervades the state of Śakti, manifesting as white and red.
The red and the white are of two kinds, and the characteristics of the feet are likewise twofold.
The red, the white, and their mixture constitute the supreme Śiva through balanced application.
When each of these resides between the two whites, there is the pair of *ṛddhi* and *siddhi*.
Initiation is in vain, knowledge is in vain, yoga is in vain, and recitation is in vain.
(I have declared that) the Śaiva and the Śākta [traditions] exist by way of the essential nature of Śiva and Śakti;
for Śakti is that which is related to Śiva, and Śiva is that which is related to Śakti.
The connection with the six-faced Īśāna arises from the power of the sixfold Śaktis;
that which originates from the manifestation of the sixfold Śaktis is proclaimed in the Śaiva and other traditions as the Samaya.

Śaiva is produced from the mouth [of the central deity]; likewise, Kālāmukha is in the south; Pāśupata is in the west; and Mahāvrata is in the north. Bhairava is said to be above that, and Vāma is declared to be in the netherworld (pātāla).
The connection with the power of Pātāla is above that, the supreme state;
the power of the directions is said to be tenfold, the arising of the divisions of the Dikcarīs.
The Dikcarī is situated in the midst of the Śakti, proclaimed as the eighth among the Guardians of the Quarters (Dikpālas);
she is born from the knots, the Mother of the Moon, who transcends Kalā, Kāla, and Vidyā.
The qualities (guṇa), the intellect (dhī), ego (garva), mind (citta), the senses (akṣi), and the subtle elements (mātrā) follow in sequence;
the first three are considered the cities of the Goddess Tripurā, and the [next] three are likewise considered her cities.
Udabhoga-hasta should be in the south-east, Mahālakṣmī in the south-west, Kubjikā-śakti in the west, and Caṇḍikā in the north-west.
In the north is Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, and in the northeast is Siddhisāmarī;
Pātāla is for the purpose of the tusk-śakti, and beyond that, in the upper direction, there shall be [the next].
This universe consists of power (śakti), yet it is the supreme Śiva who transcends the universe.
Between Śiva and Śakti, Nāda and Bindu arise;
between Nāda and Bindu, the fivefold Sādākhya arises.
The five known as the Sādās are declared to be situated in the center of the eight Vidyeśvaras;
the eight Vidyeśvaras are declared to be in the center of Rudra.
Within Rudra, situated in his own center, there arises Viṣṇu with sixty crores;
within Viṣṇu, situated in his own center, there arises Brahmā with one hundred crores.
